author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Reliquas vero partes diei tu consumebas iis delectationibus, quas tibi ipse ad arbitrium tuum compararas, nobis autem erant ea perpetienda, quae Sp. Maecius probavisset.
question: Quis fabulas probabat, quae in ludis Pompei agerentur, ut Cicero ad M. Marium scribit?
question_en: Who approved the plays that were staged at Pompey's games, as Cicero writes to M. Marius?
derivation: Sp. Maecius Tarpa, the official selector of plays for the stage (the same man Horace names as the judge of new drama). Cicero says the audience had to endure whatever Maecius had approved. Anchored to Pompey's games of 55 BC; single named answer, verbatim in the source.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: deliciae vero tuae, noster Aesopus, eiusmodi fuit, ut ei desinere per omnes homines liceret: is iurare cum coepisset, vox eum defecit in illo loco: "si sciens fallo."
question: Cuius histrionis vox in ludis Pompei defecit, cum in scaena iurare coepisset?
question_en: Which actor's voice failed him at Pompey's games, when he had begun to swear an oath on stage?
derivation: The famous tragic actor Aesopus, Cicero's friend, broke down at the oath-words 'si sciens fallo' during Pompey's dedication games. Closed-book: Aesopus is the best-known Roman tragic actor of the age; anchored to him and to the games; short named answer.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: quid enim delectationis habent sexcenti muli in Clytaemnestra aut in Equo Troiano creterrarum tria milia aut armatura varia peditatus et equitatus in aliqua pugna?
question: Quot mulos in Clytaemnestra fabula in scaenam productos esse Cicero commemorat?
question_en: How many mules does Cicero record as brought on stage in the play Clytaemnestra?
derivation: The absurd processional splendour of Pompey's games: six hundred mules in Accius' Clytaemnestra. Number fact, verbatim in the source, anchored to the named play.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: quid enim delectationis habent sexcenti muli in Clytaemnestra aut in Equo Troiano creterrarum tria milia aut armatura varia peditatus et equitatus in aliqua pugna?
question: Quot creterrae in Equo Troiano fabula in scaenam illatae sunt, ut Cicero scribit?
question_en: How many mixing-bowls were carried onto the stage in the play Equos Troianus, as Cicero writes?
derivation: Companion number to the six hundred mules: three thousand craters paraded in the Equos Troianus at Pompey's games. Anchored to the named play; verbatim number.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: non enim te puto Graecos aut Oscos ludos desiderasse, praesertim cum Oscos vel in senatu vestro spectare possis, Graecos ita non ames, ut ne ad villam quidem tuam via Graeca ire soleas.
question: Praeter Graecos, cuius gentis ludos in muneribus Pompei actos esse Cicero commemorat?
question_en: Besides Greek shows, which people's plays does Cicero mention as performed at Pompey's games?
derivation: The Oscan farces (Atellanae) alongside Greek performances in the programme of Pompey's games - a standing genre of the Roman stage. Closed-book cultural fact about Roman theatre; answer verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Reliquae sunt venationes binae per dies quinque, magnificae - nemo negat -, sed quae potest homini esse polito delectatio, cum aut homo imbecillus a valentissima bestia laniatur aut praeclara bestia venabulo transverberatur?
question: Per quot dies venationes in ludis Pompei editae sunt?
question_en: For how many days were the beast-hunts held at Pompey's games?
derivation: Number fact about the venatio at the dedication games of Pompey's theatre in 55 BC: two hunts a day for five days. Verbatim in the source; anchored to Pompey's games.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Extremus elephantorum dies fuit: in quo admiratio magna vulgi atque turbae, delectatio nulla exstitit; quin etiam misericordia quaedam consecuta est atque opinio eiusmodi, esse quandam illi beluae cum genere humano societatem.
question: Quae bestiae ultimo ludorum Pompei die in harenam productae sunt?
question_en: Which beasts were brought into the arena on the last day of Pompey's games?
derivation: The celebrated elephant show that closed Pompey's games of 55 BC (also told by Pliny). Anchored to the games; short answer, verbatim support.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Extremus elephantorum dies fuit: in quo admiratio magna vulgi atque turbae, delectatio nulla exstitit; quin etiam misericordia quaedam consecuta est atque opinio eiusmodi, esse quandam illi beluae cum genere humano societatem.
question: Quem affectum vulgus Romanum erga elephantos in ludis Pompei concepit, ut Cicero scribit?
question_en: What feeling did the Roman crowd conceive towards the elephants at Pompey's games, as Cicero writes?
derivation: The famous reaction of the crowd: pity, and a sense that the beasts had some kinship with mankind. Distinct fact from the mere staging of the elephants; verbatim support; anchored to Pompey's games.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Nam quid ego te athletas putem desiderare, qui gladiatores contempseris? in quibus ipse Pompeius confitetur se et operam et oleum perdidisse.
question: Quo proverbio Pompeius de gladiatoribus suis usum esse Cicero refert?
answer: Se et operam et oleum perdidisse.
question_en: What proverb does Cicero report Pompey using about his own gladiators?
answer_en: That he had wasted both his labour and his oil.
derivation: The standing Roman proverb 'operam et oleum perdere' (to waste labour and lamp-oil), here in Pompey's mouth about the gladiators of his games. Checkable point: who said it, and of what.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: De Bursa te gaudere certo scio; sed nimis verecunde mihi gratularis; putas enim, ut scribis, propter hominis sordes minus me magnam illam laetitiam putare. Credas mihi velim magis me iudicio hoc quam morte inimici laetatum.
question: Cuius damnatione Cicero se magis quam inimici morte laetatum esse scribit?
question_en: At whose condemnation does Cicero write that he rejoiced more than at the death of his enemy?
derivation: The condemnation of T. Munatius Plancus Bursa in 52 BC, prosecuted by Cicero; he says the verdict pleased him more than the death of his enemy (Clodius). Named entity, single verifiable answer.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Nos hic in multitudine et crebritate iudiciorum et novis legibus ita distinemur, ut quotidie vota faciamus, ne intercaletur, ut quam primum te videre possimus.
question: Quid Cicero cotidianis votis deprecabatur, ut M. Marium quam primum videre posset?
question_en: What did Cicero pray daily against, so that he might see M. Marius as soon as possible?
answer_en: That the year should not be given an intercalary month.
derivation: The pre-Julian calendar, in which the pontiffs inserted an intercalary month at their discretion and so lengthened the business year. Ambient Roman civic knowledge; anchored to Cicero and Marius; verbatim 'ne intercaletur'.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: accedit etiam, quod familiam ducit in iure civili singulari memoria, summa scientia.
question: In qua disciplina C. Trebatium Testam principem esse Cicero ad Caesarem scribens affirmat?
question_en: In what field does Cicero, writing to Caesar, declare C. Trebatius Testa to be the leader?
derivation: Trebatius Testa, the jurist to whom Cicero later dedicated the Topica, is commended to Caesar as leading the field in ius civile. Anchored to Trebatius; single short answer, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Mitto igitur ad te Trebatium atque ita mitto, ut initio mea sponte, post autem invitatu tuo mittendum duxerim. Hunc, mi Caesar, sic velim omni tua comitate complectare, ut omnia, quae per me possis adduci ut in meos conferre velis, in unum hunc conferas.
question: Ad quem imperatorem Cicero C. Trebatium Testam commendatum misit?
question_en: To which commander did Cicero send C. Trebatius Testa with a letter of recommendation?
derivation: The commendatio that sent Trebatius to Caesar's staff in Gaul and set the scene of the whole seventh book. Caesar is addressed by name in the quoted words; named entities on both sides.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: hoc tibi tam ignoscemus nos amici, quam ignoverunt Medeae, quae Corinthum arcem altam habebant matronae opulentae, optimates, quibus illa manibus gypsatissimis persuasit, ne sibi vitio illae verterent, quod abesset a patria.
question: Cuius urbis matronae opulentae Medeae, quod a patria abesset, ignoverunt?
question_en: The wealthy matrons of which city forgave Medea for being away from her homeland?
derivation: The chorus of rich Corinthian matrons whom Medea addresses in the Latin Medea (Ennius, after Euripides), quoted here by Cicero. Canonical shared myth-and-stage knowledge; single place-name answer, verbatim in the quoted verses.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Tu, qui ceteris cavere didicisti, in Britannia ne ab essedariis decipiaris caveto.
question: A quo genere pugnatorum Britannorum Cicero Trebatium in Britannia cavere iubet?
question_en: Against which kind of British fighters does Cicero warn Trebatius to be on his guard in Britain?
derivation: The essedarii, the chariot-borne warriors of Britain that Caesar's army met - ambient knowledge of the British expedition, later the name of a gladiator type at Rome. Anchored to Trebatius and Britain; verbatim answer.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: In Britannia nihil esse audio neque auri neque argenti: id si ita est, essedum aliquod capias suadeo et ad nos quam primum recurras.
question: Quas duas res in Britannia deesse Cicero se audivisse scribit?
question_en: Which two things does Cicero write that he hears are lacking in Britain?
derivation: Cicero's report on the profitlessness of the British expedition of 54 BC. Anchored to Britain; two-item verbatim answer; a claim particular to this author, framed with 'audio'.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: In Britannia nihil esse audio neque auri neque argenti: id si ita est, essedum aliquod capias suadeo et ad nos quam primum recurras.
question: Quod praedae genus Cicero Trebatio ex Britannia reportandum esse iocatur?
question_en: What kind of booty does Cicero joke that Trebatius should bring back from Britain?
derivation: Since Britain has no gold or silver, Cicero jokes that Trebatius should capture an esseda instead - the British chariot as the one prize worth taking. Anchored to Trebatius and Britain; single-word answer, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: una mehercule nostra vel severa vel iocosa congressio pluris erit quam non modo hostes, sed etiam fratres nostri Aedui.
question: Quam Galliae gentem Romani fratres suos appellabant?
question_en: Which people of Gaul did the Romans call their brothers?
derivation: The Aedui held the official style of 'brothers and kinsmen' of the Roman people, a standing formula of Roman diplomacy in Gaul; Cicero uses it in passing as common knowledge. Verbatim support, single named answer.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: denique, si cito te rettuleris, sermo nullus erit, si diutius frustra afueris, non modo Laberium, sed etiam sodalem nostrum Valerium pertimesco; mira enim persona induci potest Britannici iureconsulti.
question: Quem mimorum scriptorem Cicero veretur ne Trebatium in scaenam ut Britannicum iureconsultum inducat?
question_en: Which writer of mimes does Cicero fear may put Trebatius on stage as the character of a 'British jurist'?
derivation: D. Laberius, the leading Roman writer of mimes, whose stock characters could be built out of any public figure. Anchored to Laberius and Trebatius; single named answer, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Ubi porro illa erit formula fiduciae: VT INTER BONOS BENE AGIER OPORTET? quis enim bonus est, qui facit nihil nisi sua causa?
question: Quibus verbis sollemnibus formula fiduciae apud Romanos concipiebatur?
answer: Ut inter bonos bene agier oportet.
question_en: In what solemn words was the Roman formula of fiducia framed?
answer_en: 'That between good men there ought to be good dealing.'
derivation: The wording of the formula fiduciae, one of the best-known clauses of Roman civil procedure; Cicero quotes it as familiar to any educated reader. Verifiable, verbatim, and translatable (nothing turns on wordplay).

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Quod ius statues COMMVNI DIVIDVNDO, cum commune nihil possit esse apud eos, qui omnia voluptate sua metiuntur?
question: Quo nomine actio illa iuris civilis appellabatur, qua res inter socios communis dividebatur?
question_en: By what name was the civil-law action called by which property held in common between partners was divided?
derivation: The actio communi dividundo, a standard head of the civil law; Cicero jokes that an Epicurean cannot administer it because nothing is truly common among pleasure-seekers. Named action, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Quomodo autem tibi placebit IOVEM LAPIDEM iurare, cum scias Iovem iratum esse nemini posse?
question: Quod ius iurandum sanctissimum Cicero commemorat, cum Trebatium Epicureum factum irridet?
question_en: What most solemn oath does Cicero mention when he mocks Trebatius for turning Epicurean?
derivation: 'Iovem lapidem iurare', the most binding of Roman oaths, sworn with the flint of Jupiter Feretrius. Ambient Roman religious knowledge; verbatim; anchored to Cicero and Trebatius.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: In Equo Troiano scis esse in extremo "sero sapiunt:" tu tamen, mi vetule, non sero.
question: In cuius fabulae exitu illud "sero sapiunt" positum esse Cicero scribit?
question_en: At the end of which play does Cicero say the words 'they grow wise too late' stand?
derivation: The proverbial tag 'sero sapiunt (Phryges)' and its home at the close of the Roman Equos Troianus. Checkable point (where the saying comes from); anchored to the named play; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Qui istinc veniunt, superbiam tuam accusant, quod negent te percontantibus respondere; sed tamen est, quod gaudeas; constat enim inter omnes neminem te uno Samarobrivae iuris peritiorem esse.
question: In quo Gallico oppido neminem Trebatio iuris peritiorem esse Cicero iocatur?
question_en: In which town of Gaul does Cicero joke that no one is more skilled in law than Trebatius?
derivation: Samarobriva (Amiens), Caesar's winter headquarters in Gaul, where Trebatius was serving. Place-name answer, verbatim; anchored to Trebatius.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: nam, quod in palimpsesto, laudo equidem parismoniam; sed miror, quid in illa chartula fuerit, quod delere malueris quam haec non scribere, nisi forte tuas formulas.
question: In quo genere chartae Trebatius epistulam scripserat, cuius parsimoniam Cicero laudat?
question_en: On what kind of writing material had Trebatius written the letter whose thrift Cicero praises?
derivation: The palimpsestus, sheet scraped clean and written over to save material - Cicero's is the earliest Latin mention. Ambient knowledge of ancient book culture; verbatim; anchored to Trebatius.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Has litteras scripsi in Pomptino, cum ad villam M. Aemilii Philemonis devertissem, ex qua iam audieram fremitum clientium meorum, quos quidem tu mihi conciliasti; nam Ulubris honoris mei causa vim maximam ranunculorum se commosse constabat.
question: Cuius oppidi ranas Cicero clientium suorum loco iocans numerat?
question_en: The frogs of which town does Cicero jokingly count as his clients?
derivation: Ulubrae, the tiny half-deserted town in the Pomptine marshes whose frogs are its only population - a standing Roman joke (Horace names it too). Anchored to Cicero's patronage joke; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: itaque, ut primum Velia navigare coepi, institui Topica Aristotela conscribere ab ipsa urbe commonitus amantissima tui: eum librum tibi misi Regio scriptum, quam planissime res illa scribi potuit.
question: Cuius philosophi Topica Cicero in navigatione conscribere instituit?
question_en: Whose Topics did Cicero set about writing up while on a voyage?
derivation: Cicero's Topica, composed from memory at sea for the jurist to whom the seventh book is largely addressed. Named work and named philosopher; verbatim support.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: itaque, ut primum Velia navigare coepi, institui Topica Aristotela conscribere ab ipsa urbe commonitus amantissima tui: eum librum tibi misi Regio scriptum, quam planissime res illa scribi potuit.
question: Ex quo Italiae oppido Cicero Topica scripta misit?
question_en: From which Italian town did Cicero send off the Topica once written?
derivation: The Topica was begun as Cicero sailed from Velia and sent from Rhegium. Place fact, verbatim, anchored to the named work.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Tu, si me audies, quem soles, has paternas possessiones tenebis - nescio quid enim Velienses verebantur -, neque Heletem, nobilem amnem, relinques nec Papirianam domum deseres.
question: Quem nobilem amnem apud Veliam Cicero Trebatium ne relinquat monet?
question_en: Which noble river at Velia does Cicero urge Trebatius not to abandon?
derivation: The Hales, the river of Velia in Lucania, called 'nobilis' by Cicero. Geographic fact anchored to Velia and Trebatius' paternal estates; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Cum ei dicerem tibi videri sponsionem illam nos sine periculo facere posse, SI BONORUM TVRPILIAE POSSESSIONEM Q. CAEPIO PRAETOR EX EDICTO SVO MIHI DEDIT, negare aiebat Servium tabulas testamenti esse eas, quas instituisset is, qui factionem testamenti non habuerit; hoc idem Offilium dicere.
question: Qui iuris consultus negabat eas tabulas testamentum esse, quas is instituisset qui testamenti factionem non haberet?
question_en: Which jurist denied that tablets counted as a will if drawn up by someone who lacked testamentary capacity?
derivation: The doctrine of testamenti factio, attributed here to Servius Sulpicius Rufus (with Ofilius agreeing) in the Turpilia case. Named jurist, single verifiable answer, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Illuseras heri inter scyphos, quod dixeram controversiam esse, possetne heres, quod futurum antea factum esset, furti recte agere. Itaque, etsi domum bene potus seroque redieram, tamen id caput, ubi haec controversia est, notavi et descriptum tibi misi, ut scires id, quod tu neminem sensisse dicebas, Sex. Aelium, M'. Manilium, M. Brutum sensisse.
question: Quos tres veteres iuris consultos Cicero heredi furti actionem dari sensisse tradit?
answer: Sex. Aelium, M'. Manilium, M. Brutum.
question_en: Which three old jurists does Cicero record as having held that an heir may bring an action for theft?
answer_en: Sextus Aelius, Manius Manilius and Marcus Brutus.
derivation: The three founders of the Roman civil law as a science (Sex. Aelius Paetus, M'. Manilius, M. Iunius Brutus), cited by Cicero on the question whether an heir can sue for a theft committed before the inheritance fell in. Verbatim, named, checkable.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Cipius, opinor, olim? "non omnibus dormio:" sic ego non omnibus, mi Galle, servio.
question: Cui viro dictum illud "non omnibus dormio" tribuitur?
question_en: To which man is the saying 'I am not asleep for everybody' attributed?
derivation: The proverbial saying of Cipius, the complaisant husband who pretended to sleep - a standing Roman byword. Checkable point (who said it); verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Habes "Sardos venales, alium alio nequiorem;" cognosti meam causam et istius salaconis iniquitatem.
question: Quod proverbium de Sardis Cicero ad M. Fadium Gallum scribens affert?
question_en: What proverb about Sardinians does Cicero quote in writing to M. Fadius Gallus?
answer_en: 'Sardinians for sale, each worse than the last.'
derivation: The proverb 'Sardi venales', said to come from the mass enslavement of Sardinians by Ti. Gracchus, applied here to the Sardinian Tigellius. Checkable saying with a fixed wording; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Nam, dum volunt isti lauti terra nata, quae lege excepta sunt, in honorem adducere, fungos, heluellas, herbas omnes ita condiunt, ut nihil possit esse suavius.
question: Quod ciborum genus lege sumptuaria exceptum erat, quod lauti illi tam suaviter condiebant?
question_en: What class of foods was exempted by the sumptuary law, and so seasoned so deliciously by the gourmands?
answer_en: Things grown from the earth (vegetables and the like).
derivation: Caesar's sumptuary law exempted produce of the soil, so the rich lavished their cooks on mushrooms, greens and herbs. Roman sumptuary legislation and its evasion - shared civic and dining knowledge; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Ita ego, qui me ostreis et muraenis facile abstinebam, a beta et a malva deceptus sum; posthac igitur erimus cautiores.
question: Quibus duobus holeribus vilibus Cicero se deceptum esse scribit?
question_en: By which two cheap vegetables does Cicero write that he was caught out?
derivation: The joke of the sumptuary-law letter: Cicero, proof against oysters and lampreys, was undone by beet and mallow at a dinner. Named foods, verbatim, anchored to Cicero.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Ita ego, qui me ostreis et muraenis facile abstinebam, a beta et a malva deceptus sum; posthac igitur erimus cautiores.
question: A quibus cibis lautis Cicero se facile abstinere solitum esse scribit?
question_en: From which luxury foods does Cicero write that he easily abstained?
derivation: Oysters and lampreys as the standing emblems of Roman luxury dining. Distinct fact from the beet-and-mallow joke; verbatim, anchored to Cicero.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: In campo certe non fuisti, cum hora secunda comitiis quaestoriis institutis sella Q. Maximi, quem illi consulem esse dicebant, posita est, quo mortuo nuntiato sella ablata est.
question: Cuius consulis mors nuntiata est, cum comitia quaestoria hora secunda haberentur, ita ut sella eius auferretur?
question_en: Whose death as consul was announced while the quaestorian elections were being held at the second hour, so that his chair was carried away?
derivation: Q. Fabius Maximus, suffect consul of 45 BC, died on the last day of his consulship; the curule chair was removed from the assembly. Named person, datable public event, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ille autem, qui comitiis tributis esset auspicatus, centuriata habuit, consulem hora septima renuntiavit, qui usque ad Kalendas Ian. esset, quae erant futurae mane postridie: ita Caninio consule scito neminem prandisse.
question: Cuius consulis brevitatem Cicero eo iocatur, quod eo consule nemo pranderit?
question_en: Whose consulship does Cicero mock by saying that under him nobody took lunch?
derivation: C. Caninius Rebilus, consul for part of a single day at the end of 45 BC - one of the most quoted jokes in Latin. Named person, verbatim support.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ille autem, qui comitiis tributis esset auspicatus, centuriata habuit, consulem hora septima renuntiavit, qui usque ad Kalendas Ian. esset, quae erant futurae mane postridie: ita Caninio consule scito neminem prandisse.
question: Qua hora diei Caninius consul renuntiatus est?
question_en: At what hour of the day was Caninius declared consul?
derivation: The hour of the declaration that made Caninius consul until the Kalends of January the next morning. Number/time fact, verbatim, anchored to the named man.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: nisi cetera, quae sunt a me in secundo libro de Oratore per Antonii personam disputata de ridiculis
question: In quo libro de Oratore et per cuius personam Cicero de ridiculis disputavit?
question_en: In which book of the De Oratore, and in whose mouth, did Cicero discuss wit and laughter?
answer_en: In the second, in the person of Antonius.
derivation: Cicero's own cross-reference to the treatment of the ridiculum in De Oratore II, spoken by M. Antonius. Named work, named speaker, verbatim; the kind of fact a reader of Cicero carries.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ut etiam, si quando aliquid dignum nostro nomine emisimus, ingemescamus, quod haec "pinnigero, non armigero in corpore tela exerceantur," ut ait Philoctetes apud Attium, "abiecta gloria."
question: Apud quem poetam Latinum Philoctetes queritur tela in pinnigero, non armigero corpore exerceri?
question_en: In which Latin poet does Philoctetes complain that his arrows are spent on feathered, not armed, bodies?
derivation: Accius' Philoctetes, a stock tragedy of the Roman stage, quoted and attributed by Cicero himself. Named poet and named character; verbatim attribution.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Feci igitur sermonem inter nos habitum in Cumano, cum esset una Pomponius: tibi dedi partes Antiochinas, quas a te probari intellexisse mihi videbar; mihi sumpsi Philonis.
question: Cuius philosophi partes Cicero in dialogo suo M. Varroni tribuit?
question_en: Whose philosophical part did Cicero assign to M. Varro in his dialogue?
derivation: The dedication of the Academica: Varro speaks for Antiochus of Ascalon, Cicero for Philo. Named work-partner and named school-head; verbatim support; a fact any reader of Cicero's philosophica carries.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Feci igitur sermonem inter nos habitum in Cumano, cum esset una Pomponius: tibi dedi partes Antiochinas, quas a te probari intellexisse mihi videbar; mihi sumpsi Philonis.
question: Cuius philosophi partes Cicero in eo dialogo, quem ad Varronem misit, sibi ipse sumpsit?
question_en: Whose philosophical part did Cicero take for himself in the dialogue he sent to Varro?
derivation: The counterpart fact: Cicero speaks for Philo of Larissa and the sceptical Academy against Varro's Antiochus. Verbatim; named philosopher; distinct from the Varro/Antiochus pair.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: tamen non alienum est dignitate tua, quod ipsi Agamemnoni, regum regi, fuit honestum, habere aliquem in consiliis capiendis Nestorem
question: Quem senem in consiliis capiendis Agamemno, regum rex, habuit?
question_en: Which old man did Agamemnon, king of kings, have to help him take counsel?
derivation: The canonical pairing of Agamemnon and his aged counsellor Nestor, used by Cicero as a self-evident comparison. Shared myth; named entities; verbatim support.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Semper amavi, ut scis, M. Brutum propter eius summum ingenium, suavissimos mores, singularem probitatem atque constantiam: tamen Idibus Martiis tantum accessit ad amorem, ut mirarer locum fuisse augendi in eo, quod mihi iampridem cumulatum etiam videbatur.
question: Quo die Cicero amorem suum erga M. Brutum mirum in modum auctum esse scribit?
question_en: On what day does Cicero write that his love for M. Brutus was wonderfully increased?
derivation: Cicero dates the increase of his affection for Brutus to the Ides of March 44 BC. Calendar date plus named person; verbatim; the best-known date in Roman history.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Quid ergo est? tamen, quamdiu hic erit noster hic praefectus moribus, parebo auctoritati tuae; cum vero aberit, ad fungos me tuos conferam.
question: Quo munere morum corrigendorum Caesarem fungi Cicero significat, cui se, dum adsit, pariturum esse dicit?
question_en: What office for the correction of morals does Cicero imply Caesar holds, and to which he says he will submit while Caesar is present?
derivation: Caesar's praefectura morum, held after the civil war, under which the sumptuary law was enforced; Cicero calls him 'noster hic praefectus moribus'. Roman institution; verbatim title.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: et, ut Servius, frater tuus, quem litteratissimum fuisse iudico, facile diceret: "hic versus Plauti non est, hic est," quod tritas aures haberet notandis generibus poetarum et consuetudine legendi
question: Cuius comici poetae versus veros a falsis Servius, Paeti frater, facile diiudicabat?
question_en: Whose comic verses could Servius, Paetus' brother, easily tell genuine from spurious?
derivation: The Roman scholarly problem of authenticating Plautine verses, and Servius Clodius' reputation for settling it by ear. Named poet, named critic; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Nunc venio ad iocationes tuas, quoniam tu secundum Oenomaum Attii, non, ut olim solebat, Atellanam, sed, ut nunc fit, mimum introduxisti.
question: Quod fabularum genus aetate Ciceronis Atellanae in exitu ludorum scaenicorum successit?
question_en: What kind of play had, in Cicero's day, replaced the Atellan farce as the afterpiece of a show?
derivation: The change of theatrical custom: the Atellana used to follow the main play, the mime now does. A convention of the Roman stage stated as common knowledge; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Nunc venio ad iocationes tuas, quoniam tu secundum Oenomaum Attii, non, ut olim solebat, Atellanam, sed, ut nunc fit, mimum introduxisti.
question: Cuius poetae Latini Oenomaum Cicero ad Paetum scribens commemorat?
question_en: Which Latin poet's Oenomaus does Cicero mention in writing to Paetus?
derivation: The tragedy Oenomaus is assigned to Accius by Cicero himself ('Oenomaum Attii'). Named play, named poet; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Hirtium ego et Dolabellam dicendi discipulos habeo, coenandi magistros; puto enim te audisse, si forte ad vos omnia perferuntur, illos apud me declamitare, me apud illos coenitare.
question: Quos duos viros Cicero dicendi discipulos, coenandi magistros se habere iocatur?
question_en: Which two men does Cicero joke that he has as pupils in speaking and masters in dining?
derivation: One of the most quoted lines of the Paetus correspondence: they declaim at Cicero's house, he dines at theirs. Named entities; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: volo enim videre animum, qui mihi audeat ista, quae scribis, apponere aut etiam polypum miniati Iovis similem.
question: Cui deo minio illito Cicero polypum in mensa appositum comparat?
question_en: To which minium-painted god does Cicero compare an octopus set on the table?
derivation: The cult statue of Jupiter Capitolinus was painted with red lead (minium) on festal days - ambient Roman religious practice, here the point of a dinner joke. Named god; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Neque est, quod in promulside spei ponas aliquid, quam totam sustuli; solebam enim antea debilitari oleis et lucanicis tuis.
question: Quo nomine prima coenae Romanae pars appellabatur, quam Cicero se totam sustulisse scribit?
question_en: What was the name of the first course of a Roman dinner, which Cicero writes that he has abolished altogether?
derivation: The promulsis, the relish course served before the mulsum at the start of a Roman dinner. Named institution of the table; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Neque est, quod in promulside spei ponas aliquid, quam totam sustuli; solebam enim antea debilitari oleis et lucanicis tuis.
question: Quibus duobus cibis in promulside appositis Cicero se antea debilitari solitum esse scribit?
question_en: By which two foods served at the hors d'oeuvre does Cicero write that he used to be laid low?
derivation: Olives and lucanicae (Lucanian sausages) as the standard opening relishes of a Roman dinner. Named dishes; verbatim; distinct fact from the course-name pair.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Tu vero - volo enim abstergere animi tui metum - ad tyrotarichum antiquum redi.
question: Ad quod ferculum vetus Cicero Paetum redire iubet, ne novam eius lautitiam extimescat?
question_en: To which old dish does Cicero tell Paetus to go back, so that he need not dread Cicero's new refinement?
derivation: The tyrotarichum, a homely dish of cheese and salt fish, the emblem of Paetus' plain table. Named dish; verbatim; anchored to Paetus.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Ego tibi unum sumptum afferam. quod balneum calfacias oportebit; cetera more nostro: superiora illa lusimus.
question: Quem unum sumptum Cicero se Paeto hospiti allaturum esse dicit?
question_en: What single expense does Cicero say he will bring upon his host Paetus?
derivation: The Roman custom of bathing before dinner: the guest's one cost to his host is the heating of the bath. Anchored to Cicero and Paetus; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ex quibus intellexi probari tibi meum consilium, quod, ut Dionysius tyrannus, cum Syracusis pulsus esset, Corinthi dicitur ludum aperuisse, sic ego sublatis iudiciis amisso regno forensi ludum quasi habere coeperim.
question: In qua urbe Dionysius tyrannus, Syracusis pulsus, ludum aperuisse dicitur?
question_en: In which city is Dionysius the tyrant said to have opened a school after being driven out of Syracuse?
derivation: The proverbial fall of Dionysius II of Syracuse, reduced to schoolmastering at Corinth. Famous story, named persons and places, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: nisi forte mori melius fuit: in lectulo, fateor, sed non accidit; in acie non fui; ceteri quidem, Pompeius, Lentulus tuus, Scipio, Afranius foede perierunt. "At Cato praeclare."
question: Cuius mortem Cicero, cum Pompei, Lentuli, Scipionis, Afranii foedos exitus commemoraret, praeclaram fuisse concedit?
question_en: Whose death does Cicero allow to have been glorious, when he lists the foul ends of Pompey, Lentulus, Scipio and Afranius?
derivation: The contrast between the squalid deaths of the Pompeian leaders and Cato's suicide at Utica - a fixed point of Roman moral history. Named entities; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Extremum illud est, quod tu nescio an primum putes: plures iam pavones confeci, quam tu pullos columbinos.
question: Quas aves Cicero se plures quam Paetus pullos columbinos confecisse iocatur?
question_en: Which birds does Cicero joke that he has polished off in greater numbers than Paetus has squabs?
derivation: The peacock as the emblematic luxury bird of the late-Republican table, set against the humble pigeon-squab. Named foods; verbatim; anchored to Cicero and Paetus.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: At quem virum! non eum, quem tu es solitus promulside conficere: integram famem ad ovum affero, itaque usque ad assum vitulinum opera perducitur.
question: A quo cibo ad quem Cicero totam coenam se perducere gloriatur?
answer: Ab ovo usque ad assum vitulinum.
question_en: From which dish to which does Cicero boast that he carries the whole dinner through?
answer_en: From the egg all the way to the roast veal.
derivation: The shape of a Roman dinner, from the egg of the gustatio to the roast that ends the main course - the phrase behind 'ab ovo usque ad mala'. Verbatim; anchored to Cicero's boast of new appetite.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: dediscendae tibi sunt sportellae et artolagani tui.
question: Quas duas res Paeto dediscendas esse Cicero scribit, cum se edacem factum esse iocatur?
question_en: Which two things does Cicero tell Paetus he must now unlearn, joking that he has become a big eater?
answer_en: His little baskets of snacks and his artolagani (bread-cakes).
derivation: Named light fare of a frugal table: the sportella (snack-hamper) and the artolaganus, a cake of flour, wine and milk. Verbatim; anchored to Paetus.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed vide audaciam: etiam Hirtio coenam dedi, sine pavone tamen; in ea coena cocus meus praeter ius fervens nihil non potuit imitari.
question: Cui Cicero coenam dedit, sine pavone tamen, ut ipse gloriatur?
question_en: To whom did Cicero give a dinner - though without a peacock - as he himself boasts?
derivation: Cicero entertaining Hirtius, one of his 'masters in dining', but stopping short of the peacock. Named guest; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Haec igitur est nunc vita nostra: mane salutamus domi et bonos viros multos, sed tristes, et hos laetos victores, qui me quidem perofficiose et peramanter observant; ubi salutatio defluxit, litteris me involvo: aut scribo aut lego.
question: Quo officio cotidiano mane domi suae Cicero fungebatur, priusquam se litteris involveret?
question_en: What daily duty did Cicero perform at home in the morning before burying himself in his books?
answer_en: The morning reception of friends (the salutatio).
derivation: The salutatio, the morning levee at a great man's house - the central ritual of Roman patronage. Named custom; verbatim; anchored to Cicero's daily routine.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: fuerunt enim patricii minorum gentium, quorum princeps L. Papirius Mugillanus, qui censor cum L. Sempronio Atratino fuit, cum ante consul cum eodem fuisset, annis post Romam conditam CCCXII.
question: Quoto anno post Romam conditam L. Papirius Mugillanus cum L. Sempronio Atratino censor fuit, ut Cicero tradit?
question_en: In which year after the founding of Rome was L. Papirius Mugillanus censor with L. Sempronius Atratinus, as Cicero records?
derivation: Cicero's dating of the first Papirian censorship, given by years from the founding of the City - the standard Roman reckoning. Named magistrates, numeric answer, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed tum Papisii dicebamini. Post hunc XIII. sederunt in sella curuli ante L. Papirium Crassum, qui primus Papisius est vocari desitus: is dictator cum L. Papirio Cursore magistro equitum factus est annis post Romam conditam CCCCXV.
question: Quo nomine Papirii antiquitus appellabantur?
question_en: By what name were the Papirii called in early times?
derivation: The older form of the gentile name, changed to Papirius; Cicero tells Paetus the family was once called Papisii. Named gens; verbatim; the fact survives translation as a name-change.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed tum Papisii dicebamini. Post hunc XIII. sederunt in sella curuli ante L. Papirium Crassum, qui primus Papisius est vocari desitus: is dictator cum L. Papirio Cursore magistro equitum factus est annis post Romam conditam CCCCXV.
question: Quis primus ex ea gente Papisius vocari desiit?
question_en: Who was the first of that family to stop being called Papisius?
derivation: Cicero names L. Papirius Crassus, dictator in the year 415 from the founding, as the first to drop the old form. Named person; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: is dictator cum L. Papirio Cursore magistro equitum factus est annis post Romam conditam CCCCXV. et quadriennio post consul cum K. Duilio.
question: Quem magistrum equitum L. Papirius Crassus dictator habuit?
question_en: Whom did the dictator L. Papirius Crassus have as his master of horse?
derivation: The pairing of dictator and magister equitum, the standing Roman constitutional arrangement, here with two Papirii. Named entities; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Tres illi fratres fuerunt, C., Cn., M. Carbones: Marcus P. Flacco accusante condemnatus est, fur magnus, ex Sicilia; Gaius accusante L. Crasso cantharidas sumpsisse dicitur: is et tribunus pl. seditiosus et P. Africano vim attulisse existimatus est.
question: Quo veneno C. Carbo, a L. Crasso accusatus, se necasse dicitur?
question_en: By what poison is C. Carbo said to have killed himself when prosecuted by L. Crassus?
derivation: The celebrated end of C. Papirius Carbo, who took cantharides when Crassus prosecuted him. Named persons; verbatim; blister-beetle poison is a known item of Roman lore.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Gaius accusante L. Crasso cantharidas sumpsisse dicitur: is et tribunus pl. seditiosus et P. Africano vim attulisse existimatus est.
question: Cui viro clarissimo vim attulisse C. Carbo existimatus est?
question_en: Against which famous man was C. Carbo thought to have laid violent hands?
derivation: The suspicion that Carbo murdered Scipio Aemilianus, a standing item of late-Republican political memory. Named persons; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: hoc vero, qui Lilybaei a Pompeio nostro est interfectus, improbior nemo meo iudicio fuit
question: In quo Siciliae oppido Cn. Carbo a Pompeio interfectus est?
question_en: In which town of Sicily was Cn. Carbo put to death by Pompey?
derivation: Pompey's execution of the consular Cn. Papirius Carbo at Lilybaeum in 81 BC, the deed that earned him the name 'adulescentulus carnifex'. Named place and persons; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Socraten fidibus docuit nobilissimus fidicen; is "Connus" vocitatus est: num id obscenum putas?
question: Quis fidicen nobilissimus Socratem fidibus docuisse dicitur?
question_en: Which most distinguished lyre-player is said to have taught Socrates the lyre?
derivation: Connus, the music-master of Socrates, a name familiar from Plato and standing in the shared Graeco-Roman anecdote stock. Named entities; verbatim; translates cleanly.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Summum me ducem litterae tuae reddiderunt: plane nesciebam te tam peritum esse rei militaris; Pyrrhi te libros et Cineae video lectitasse.
question: Quorum duorum virorum libros de re militari Cicero Paetum lectitasse iocatur?
question_en: Whose two books on the art of war does Cicero joke that Paetus has been reading?
derivation: The military handbooks of King Pyrrhus and of his minister Cineas, the standard ancient works on tactics. Named authors; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Accubueram hora nona, cum ad te harum exemplum in codicillis exaravi. Dices: "ubi?" Apud Volumnium Eutrapelum, et quidem supra me Atticus, infra Verrius, familiares tui.
question: Qua hora diei Cicero apud Volumnium Eutrapelum ad coenam accubuit?
question_en: At what hour of the day did Cicero recline for dinner at the house of Volumnius Eutrapelus?
derivation: The ninth hour as the usual time for a Roman dinner party to begin. Named host, precise hour, verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Audi reliqua: infra Eutrapelum Cytheris accubuit.
question: Quae mulier famosa in convivio Volumni Eutrapeli, cui Cicero interfuit, infra ipsum hospitem accubuit?
question_en: Which notorious woman reclined below the host himself at Volumnius Eutrapelus' dinner, at which Cicero was present?
derivation: Volumnia Cytheris, the celebrated mime-actress and mistress of Antony, at table with Cicero - one of the best-known scenes of the correspondence. Named person; verbatim; couch-order is Roman dining custom.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed tamen ne Aristippus quidem ille Socraticus erubuit, cum esset obiectum habere eum Laida: "habeo," inquit, "non habeor a Laide"
question: Quid Aristippus Socraticus respondit, cum ei obiceretur Laida habere?
question_en: What did Aristippus the Socratic reply when he was reproached with keeping Lais?
answer_en: 'I possess her, I am not possessed by her.'
derivation: The famous retort of Aristippus of Cyrene about the courtesan Lais, quoted by Cicero as common property. Checkable saying with a named speaker; editorial supplement 'a Laide' unbracketed per the normalization rule.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: De Tirone, mi Marce, ita te meumque Ciceronem et tuam Tulliolam tuumque filium videam, ut mihi gratissimum fecisti, quod eum, indignum illa fortuna ac nobis amicum quam servum esse maluisti.
question: Quem servum M. Cicero, ut Quintus frater ei gratulatur, amicum potius quam servum esse maluit?
question_en: Which slave did M. Cicero prefer to have as a friend rather than a slave, as his brother Quintus congratulates him?
derivation: The manumission of Tiro, Cicero's secretary, congratulated by Quintus - the best-known Roman manumission of a household slave. Named entities; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Video, quid agas: tuas quoque epistulas vis referri in volumina.
question: Quid Tiro de suis quoque epistulis fieri velle a Cicerone deprehenditur?
question_en: What does Cicero catch Tiro wanting to be done with his own letters too?
answer_en: That they be collected into volumes.
derivation: The Roman practice of gathering correspondence into published rolls - the practice that produced the Ad Familiares itself, with Tiro as its likely editor. Named entities; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed tamen Asclapo medicus plane confirmat propediem te valentem fore.
question: Quis medicus Ciceroni confirmavit Tironem brevi valiturum esse?
question_en: Which doctor assured Cicero that Tiro would soon be well?
derivation: Asclapo of Patrae, the physician who attended Tiro during his long illness. Named doctor and named patient; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sed, quoniam in quartanam conversa vis est morbi - sic enim scribit Curius -, spero te diligentia adhibita iam firmiorem fore.
question: In quod febris genus Tironis morbus conversus est, ut Curius ad Ciceronem scripsit?
question_en: Into what kind of fever had Tiro's illness turned, as Curius wrote to Cicero?
derivation: The quartana, the four-day-cycle fever of ancient medicine, thought a milder turn of a serious illness. Named condition; named patient and informant; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: A. d. XV K. in portum Corcyraeorum ad Cassiopen stadia CXX processimus; ibi retenti ventis sumus usque ad a. d. VIIII K. - interea, qui cupide profecti sunt, multi naufragia fecerunt -. Nos eo die coenati solvimus; inde austro lenissimo, caelo sereno nocte illa et die postero in Italiam ad Hydruntem ludibundi pervenimus.
question: Ex quo Corcyraeorum portu Cicero in Italiam ad Hydruntem traiecit?
question_en: From which harbour of the Corcyraeans did Cicero cross to Hydruntum in Italy?
derivation: The standard crossing from Cassiope on Corcyra to Hydruntum (Otranto), the shortest passage between Greece and Italy. Named ports; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Antonius quidem noster et Q. Cassius nulla vi expulsi ad Caesarem cum Curione profecti erant
question: Qui duo tribuni plebis cum Curione ad Caesarem initio belli civilis profecti sunt?
question_en: Which two tribunes of the plebs set out with Curio to join Caesar at the beginning of the civil war?
derivation: The flight of the tribunes Antony and Q. Cassius to Caesar in January 49 BC, Caesar's stated casus belli. Named persons; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: posteaquam senatus consulibus, praetoribus, tribunis pl. et nobis, qui pro coss. sumus, negotium dederat, ut curaremus, ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet
question: Quibus verbis sollemnibus senatus magistratibus summam rei publicae tuendae mandabat?
answer: Ut viderent ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet.
question_en: In what solemn words did the senate charge the magistrates with the safety of the state?
answer_en: 'That they see to it that the state take no harm.'
derivation: The wording of the senatus consultum ultimum, the emergency decree of the Roman senate, quoted here as Cicero reports its passage in January 49 BC. Fixed institutional formula; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Italiae regiones descriptae sunt, quam quisque partem tueretur: nos Capuam sumpsimus.
question: Quam Italiae partem Cicero initio belli civilis tuendam sibi sumpsit?
question_en: Which part of Italy did Cicero take for himself to defend at the beginning of the civil war?
derivation: The division of Italy into defence zones among the Pompeian leaders in 49 BC, with Capua assigned to Cicero. Named place and person; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Itaque, quum Caesar amentia quadam raperetur et oblitus nominis atque honorum suorum Ariminum, Pisaurum, Anconam, Arretium occupavisset, urbem reliquimus
question: Quae quattuor Italiae oppida Caesarem occupavisse Cicero scribit, priusquam senatus urbem relinqueret?
question_en: Which four Italian towns does Cicero say Caesar had seized before the senate abandoned Rome?
derivation: Caesar's first seizures on crossing the Rubicon in January 49 BC, listed by Cicero as they were reported at Rome. Named places; verbatim; one coherent answer.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ad consulatus petitionem se venturum, neque se iam velle absente se rationem haberi suam; se praesentem trinum nundinum petiturum.

question_en: For what legally prescribed period did Caesar promise to canvass for the consulship in person?
derivation: The trinum nundinum, the interval of three market-days that Roman law required for a candidacy or a bill. Named institution; verbatim; anchored to Caesar's terms of January 49 BC.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Maximam autem plagam accepit, quod is, qui summam auctoritatem in illius exercitu habebat, T. Labienus, socius sceleris esse noluit: reliquit illum et nobiscum est, multique idem facturi esse dicuntur.
question: Quis legatus, qui in Caesaris exercitu summam auctoritatem habebat, initio belli civilis ad Pompeianos transiit?
question_en: Which officer, who held the highest authority in Caesar's army, went over to the Pompeians at the start of the civil war?
derivation: Labienus' desertion of Caesar in 49 BC, the most famous defection of the war. Named person; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: ex Hispaniaque sex legiones et magna auxilia Afranio et Petreio ducibus habet a tergo
question: Qui duo duces sex legionibus in Hispania praeerant, quas Cicero Caesari a tergo esse scribit?
question_en: Which two commanders led the six legions in Spain that Cicero says stood at Caesar's back?
derivation: Pompey's Spanish army under L. Afranius and M. Petreius, later defeated at Ilerda. Named commanders, troop number; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: putabamusque illum metuere, si ad urbem ire coepisset, ne Gallias amitteret, quas ambas habet inimicissimas praeter Transpadanos
question: Quos solos Galliae incolas Caesari non inimicos fuisse Cicero scribit?
question_en: Which inhabitants of Gaul alone does Cicero say were not hostile to Caesar?
derivation: The Transpadani, Caesar's clients north of the Po whose enfranchisement he championed - the one friendly element in his provinces. Named people; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: Quum vehementer tabellarios exspectarem quotidie, aliquando venerunt post diem quadragesimum et sextum, quam a vobis discesserant
question: Post quot dies tabellarii ab Italia missi ad M. Ciceronem filium Athenas pervenerunt?

derivation: The speed of private correspondence between Italy and Athens - forty-six days for the tabellarii. Number fact; verbatim (editorial brackets round 'et' removed per the normalization rule); anchored to Cicero's son at Athens.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI

derivation: Cratippus the Peripatetic, under whom Cicero's son studied at Athens and to whom the De Officiis sends him. Named persons; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI

question: Cuius rhetoris cotidianam declamationem M. Cicero filius Athenis patris iussu deposuit?

derivation: The dismissal of the rhetor Gorgias at the elder Cicero's command, a well-attested episode of the son's Athenian studies. Named persons; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: videor enim videre ementem te rusticas res, cum villico loquentem, in lacinia servantem ex mensa secunda semina.
question: Ex qua coenae parte semina Tiro in lacinia servare fingitur?
question_en: From which part of the dinner is Tiro imagined saving seeds in the fold of his garment?
derivation: The mensa secunda, the fruit-and-sweet course that closed a Roman dinner - hence the seeds Tiro the new landowner pockets for planting. Named course; verbatim.

author: Cicero
work: Epistulae ad Familiares, libri VII, IX, XVI
source_text: sicut olim matrem nostram facere memini, quae lagonas etiam inanes obsignabat, ne dicerentur inanes aliquae fuisse, quae furtim essent exsiccatae
question: Quas res etiam inanes matrem Ciceronum obsignare solitam esse Quintus meminit?
question_en: What did Quintus remember the Ciceros' mother sealing even when they were empty?
derivation: The household practice of sealing wine-jars so that pilfering by the slaves could be detected - Quintus' mother sealed even the empty ones. Named object; verbatim; a custom of Roman domestic management.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: The rudis, the wooden foil handed to a gladiator on discharge, is the standing Roman image of retirement; Horace applies it to himself in the opening lines of the Epistulae. Anchored to Horace + Maecenas; one-word answer stated verbatim (donatum iam rude). Translatable and culturally salient: arena custom every Roman knew.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Non eadem est aetas, non mens. Veianius armis Herculis ad postem fixis latet abditus agro, ne populum extrema totiens exoret harena.

derivation: Retiring gladiators dedicated their weapons at the doorpost of Hercules, patron of the arena. Anchored to the named gladiator Veianius; single-name answer stated verbatim (Herculis ad postem fixis). Closed-book cult-and-spectacle custom, not passage-dependent.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Non possis oculo quantum contendere Lynceus, non tamen idcirco contemnas lippus inungui;

derivation: Lynceus the Argonaut is the canonical byword for sharp sight. Anchored by name; short answer supported verbatim. Shared mythological knowledge, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: The equestrian census of 400,000 sesterces, the threshold of the ordo equester. Anchored to the Roman census classes; a single number, stated verbatim (quadringentis... desunt: plebs eris). Institutional fact of Roman society, closed-book and translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: What did Roman boys chant to one another at play, as Horace reports?
answer_en: 'You shall be king, if you do right.'
derivation: A children's game-formula of Roman childhood, quoted verbatim by Horace. Anchored to Roman boys at play + Horace; short quoted answer supported verbatim. Ambient custom, not doctrine.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: olim quod uolpes aegroto cauta leoni respondit, referam: 'Quia me uestigia terrent, omnia te aduersum spectantia, nulla retrorsum.'

answer: Quia omnia vestigia ad leonem spectabant, nulla retrorsum.
question_en: Why, in the fable Horace tells, did the wary fox refuse to go in to the sick lion?
answer_en: Because all the tracks pointed toward the lion, none back out.
derivation: The Aesopic fable of the sick lion and the fox, a shared story of the ancient world, quoted by Horace. Anchored to the named animals + the fable; answer stated verbatim. Short and checkable; not a moral.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: Which sea-god, changing his shape, does Horace complain cannot be held by any knot?
derivation: Proteus the shape-shifting sea-god, canonical myth. Anchored by name; one-word answer supported verbatim. Culturally salient shared story; translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: Horace's re-reading of Homer at Praeneste, the frame of Epistle 1.2. Anchored to Horace + Lollius + the poet of the Trojan war; single place-name answer stated verbatim. Closed-book fact of literary biography and geography.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quicquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achiui.
question: In cuius belli exemplo Horatius illud 'quidquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi' protulit?
question_en: Apropos of which war did Horace produce the tag 'whatever folly the kings commit, the Achaeans pay for it'?
derivation: One of Horace's most quoted tags, drawn in Epistle 1.2 from his reading of the Iliad (the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon, Paris' love, the walls of Troy). Anchored to the tag itself; the answer names the war the epistle is expounding. The Latin Library file prints 'Qucquid' for 'Quicquid', an evident typo of the conversion, corrected here.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: The Odyssey's two great temptations named by Horace as common knowledge. Anchored to Ulysses + the Sirens; single-name answer supported verbatim. Shared myth, translatable.

derivation: A famous Horatian tag, whose checkable point is its authorship and place (Epistulae 1.2, to Lollius). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer, supported verbatim by the source line.

author: Horace

derivation: The tag sapere aude, later the motto of the Enlightenment, stands in Horace's Epistle 1.2 beside dimidium facti. Anchored to Horace + Lollius + the neighbouring tag; the two-word answer is verbatim in the source.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: Ira furor brevis est, one of the best-known Latin sayings; the checkable fact is who wrote it (Horace, Epistulae 1.2). Anchored to the saying; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace

derivation: Tiberius as privignus of Augustus (son of Livia by her first husband). Anchored to both named men; short answer stated verbatim. Closed-book fact of the Augustan house.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: From which Greek poet's spring does Horace say Titius did not turn pale to drink?
derivation: Pindar as the perilous model for Latin lyric, a standing Augustan literary judgement. Anchored to Titius + the Pindaric spring; single-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: In which god's temple on the Palatine were the writings kept that Horace warns Celsus not to touch?
derivation: The library in the temple of Palatine Apollo, Augustus' great public collection. Anchored to Celsus + the Palatine temple; single-name answer stated verbatim. Institutional fact of Augustan Rome.

author: Horace

question_en: Which bird, in the fable, raises a laugh when it is stripped of its stolen colours as the other birds take back their feathers?
derivation: The Aesopic fable of the crow in borrowed plumage, cited by Horace as a warning against plagiarism. Anchored to the fable; one-word answer stated verbatim. Shared story, translatable.

author: Horace

question_en: By what joking name does Horace call himself in the letter to Albius, alluding to the school of Epicurus?
derivation: Horace's celebrated self-description, the standing joke about Epicureans. Anchored to Horace + Albius + Epicurus; short answer quoted verbatim from the source line.

author: Horace

derivation: Roman wine was dated by the consuls of its vintage; Horace names Statilius Taurus' second consulship. Anchored to Horace + Torquatus + the named vintage; short answer stated verbatim. Food-and-drink culture, translatable.

author: Horace

question_en: Whose birthday makes the holiday on which Horace invites Torquatus to dinner?
derivation: The emperor's birthday as a public holiday, an Augustan institution of the calendar. Anchored to Horace's invitation + the named Caesar; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Tu quotus esse uelis rescribe, et rebus omissis atria seruantem postico falle clientem.

derivation: The client waiting in the atrium and the patron slipping out by the back door: the daily mechanics of Roman patronage. Anchored to Torquatus + his client; short answer stated verbatim (postico).

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: Of what colour are the lictors that Horace says attend the funeral marshal?
derivation: The dissignator, master of ceremonies at Roman funerals, walked with black-clad lictors. Anchored to the named office; one-word answer stated verbatim. Funerary custom, the heart of criterion 8.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: A host of which region of Italy, in Horace, presses his guest to eat pears that he would otherwise leave to the pigs?
derivation: The 'Calabrian host' is Horace's proverbial figure of grudging, worthless generosity. Anchored to the named region + the pears; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace

question_en: Which animal, in Horace, advised the little fox shut in the corn-bin to come out thin as it had gone in thin?
derivation: The fable of the fox in the corn-bin and the weasel's advice, a shared Aesopic story. Anchored to the fox + the corn-bin; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Haud male Telemachus, proles patientis Vlixei: 'Non est aptus equis Ithace locus, ut neque planis porrectus spatiis nec multae prodigus herbae;

question_en: Why, in Horace, does Telemachus refuse the horses offered him by the son of Atreus?
answer_en: Because Ithaca is no place for horses.
derivation: The Odyssean scene of Telemachus at Sparta declining Menelaus' horses because rocky Ithaca cannot pasture them. Anchored to Telemachus + Ithaca; short answer stated verbatim. Shared story, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question_en: At about what hour of the day did the advocate Philippus return home from his business, as Horace tells it?

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: The praeco, the auctioneer-crier of Roman public life, is the trade of Horace's Volteius Mena. Anchored to the named man; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

author: Horace

author: Horace

derivation: The sum of Horace's cautionary tale: seven sestertia given and seven lent. Anchored to the two named men + the farm; a single number stated verbatim.

author: Horace

question: Cuius poetae Romani praeceptum est illud 'nil admirari', ad Numicium scriptum?
question_en: Which Roman poet's precept is the famous 'nil admirari', written to Numicius?
derivation: The tag nil admirari, one of the most quoted phrases in Latin; the checkable point is its author and addressee (Horace, Epistulae 1.6, to Numicius). Anchored to the quoted words + the named addressee; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

question: Cuius viri porticum Horatius una cum via Appia inter celeberrima Romae loca nominat?

derivation: The Porticus Agrippae and the Via Appia as the two places where a well-known man is seen: Augustan topography of Rome. Anchored to the named monuments; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

derivation: The anecdote of Lucullus' proverbial wealth (he is named two lines above: Chlamydes Lucullus, ut aiunt): asked for a hundred stage-cloaks, he finds five thousand at home. Anchored to Lucullus + the request; a single number stated verbatim.

author: Horace

answer_en: He prompted the names of those they met.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Si, Mimnermus uti censet, sine amore iocisque nil est iucundum, uiuas in amore iocisque.
question: Cuius poetae Graeci sententia est nihil sine amore iocisque iucundum esse, ut Horatius refert?
question_en: Which Greek poet held, as Horace reports, that nothing is pleasant without love and jesting?
derivation: Mimnermus of Colophon, the elegist of love and pleasure, cited by name. Anchored to Horace + the doctrine attributed; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary-cultural fact, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Naturam expelles furca, tamen usque recurret et mala perrumpet furtim fastidia uictrix.
question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit naturam furca expulsam usque recursuram esse?
question_en: Which Roman poet wrote that nature, though driven out with a pitchfork, will always come running back?
derivation: Naturam expelles furca, one of the most quoted Latin proverbs; the checkable point is its author (Horace, Epistulae 1.10, to Aristius Fuscus). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Haec tibi dictabam post fanum putre Vacunae, excepto quod non simul esses cetera laetus.
question: Cuius deae fanum apud agrum Sabinum Horatius nominat, unde epistulam ad Aristium Fuscum dictavit?
question_en: Whose shrine in the Sabine country does Horace name as the place from which he dictated the letter to Aristius Fuscus?
derivation: Vacuna, the old Sabine goddess whose crumbling shrine stood near Horace's farm. Anchored to Horace + the Sabine country; one-name answer stated verbatim. Local cult knowledge of the sort a Roman reader carried.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quid tibi uisa Chios, Bullati, notaque Lesbos, quid concinna Samos, quid Croesi regia Sardis, Zmyrna quid et Colophon?
question: Cuius regis regiam urbem Horatius Sardis appellat?
question_en: Whose royal city does Horace call Sardis?
derivation: Sardis as the seat of Croesus, the byword for royal wealth. Anchored to the named city; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared geographical-historical knowledge.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Scis Lebedus quid sit: Gabiis desertior atque Fidenis uicus; tamen illic uiuere uellem,
question: Quibus duobus Latii oppidis desertioribus Horatius Lebedum comparat?
question_en: With which two towns of Latium does Horace compare Lebedus, saying it is emptier than they?
derivation: Gabii and Fidenae as the proverbially deserted towns of Latium. Anchored to Lebedus + the comparison; two named places stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: caelum, non animum mutant, qui trans mare currunt.
question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit eos qui trans mare currunt caelum, non animum mutare?
question_en: Which Roman poet wrote that those who race across the sea change their sky, not their mind?
derivation: A celebrated Horatian tag from the letter to Bullatius; the checkable point is its author and work. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quod petis, hic est, est Vlubris, animus si te non deficit aequus.
question: Quod oppidum parvum Horatius nominat, ubi quod petimus inveniri possit, si animus aequus non desit?
question_en: Which small town does Horace name as a place where what we seek can be found, if a balanced mind does not fail us?
derivation: Ulubrae, the tiny Pomptine town, proverbial for obscurity, in one of Horace's most quoted closes. Anchored to the tag; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Fructibus Agrippae Siculis quos colligis, Icci, si recte frueris, non est ut copia maior ab Ioue donari possit tibi;
question: Cuius viri fructus Siculos Iccius colligebat, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: Whose Sicilian revenues was Iccius collecting, as Horace writes?
derivation: Iccius as steward of Agrippa's Sicilian estates. Anchored to the two named men; one-name answer stated verbatim. Fact of Augustan property and patronage.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Miramur, si Democriti pecus edit agellos cultaque, dum peregre est animus sine corpore uelox,
question: Cuius philosophi pecus agellos depastum esse fertur, dum animus eius peregre abest?
question_en: Whose fields, as the story goes, were eaten up by his own flocks while his mind was away abroad?
derivation: The anecdote of Democritus so absorbed in thought that his flocks ate his crops. Anchored to the named philosopher; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared biographical lore.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Cantaber Agrippae, Claudi uirtute Neronis Armenius cecidit;
question: Cuius ducis virtute Cantaber cecidit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
question_en: By which commander's valour did the Cantabrian fall, as Horace writes to Iccius?
derivation: Agrippa's Cantabrian victory of 19 BC, reported by Horace as the news from Rome. Anchored to the Cantabri + Horace's letter; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Cantaber Agrippae, Claudi uirtute Neronis Armenius cecidit;
question: Cuius virtute Armenius cecidit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
question_en: By whose valour did the Armenian fall, as Horace writes to Iccius?
derivation: Tiberius' Armenian settlement of 20 BC. Anchored to the Armenians + Horace's letter; name stated verbatim (Claudi uirtute Neronis).

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: ius imperiumque Prahates Caesaris accepit genibus minor;
question: Quis rex, genibus minor, ius imperiumque Caesaris accepit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
question_en: Which king, on bended knee, accepted Caesar's law and sway, as Horace writes to Iccius?
derivation: Phraates IV of Parthia submitting to Augustus, the diplomatic triumph of 20 BC. Anchored to Caesar + the submission; one-name answer stated verbatim in the Latin Library's spelling Prahates.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vilice siluarum et mihi me reddentis agelli, quem tu fastidis habitatum quinque focis et quinque bonos solitum Variam dimittere patres,
question: Quot patres familias fundus Horati Sabinus Variam mittere solebat?
question_en: How many heads of household did Horace's Sabine estate regularly send down to Varia?
derivation: The size of Horace's Sabine farm: five hearths, five tenant fathers who sat in the council at Varia. Anchored to Horace's farm + Varia; a single number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nam mihi Baias Musa superuacuas Antonius, et tamen illis me facit inuisum, gelida cum perluor unda per medium frigus;
question: Cuius medici auctoritate Horatius Baias supervacuas habuit, gelida potius unda perfusus?
question_en: On which physician's authority did Horace treat Baiae as superfluous, washing instead in cold water?
derivation: Antonius Musa, Augustus' doctor, whose cold-water regimen turned Roman fashion away from the warm springs of Baiae. Anchored to Horace + Baiae; name stated verbatim. Salient fact of Augustan medicine and fashion.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sulpura contemni uicus gemit, inuidus aegris qui caput et stomachum supponere fontibus audent Clusinis Gabiosque petunt et frigida rura.
question: Ad quorum locorum frigidos fontes aegri se conferebant, spretis Baiarum sulphuribus, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: To the cold springs of which places did the sick betake themselves, scorning the sulphur baths of Baiae, as Horace writes?
answer_en: To the springs of Clusium and to Gabii.
derivation: The cold-water cure that displaced Baiae: the springs of Clusium and Gabii. Anchored to Baiae + the invalids; two place-names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aiebat, 'si qui comedunt bona, cum sit obeso nil melius turdo, nil uolua pulchrius ampla'.
question: Quas duas res in cena optimas esse Maenius apud Horatium dicebat?
question_en: Which two things did Maenius, in Horace, call the best at dinner?
answer_en: A fat thrush and a large sow's womb.
derivation: The two canonical delicacies of the Roman table, in the mouth of Horace's glutton Maenius (named at 1.15.26). Anchored to Maenius + the dinner; both items stated verbatim. Food culture, criterion 8's home ground.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: 'Nec furtum feci nec fugi,' si mihi dicat seruos: 'Habes pretium, loris non ureris', aio. 'Non hominem occidi.' 'Non pasces in cruce coruos.'
question: Quod supplicium servum, qui hominem occidisset, apud Romanos manebat, ut Horatius indicat?
question_en: What punishment awaited a slave who had killed a man, as Horace indicates?
derivation: Crucifixion as the servile penalty (and the lash for theft). Anchored to the slave's plea; one-word answer stated verbatim (non pasces in cruce coruos). Legal and social fact, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: labra mouet, metuens audiri: 'Pulchra Lauerna, da mihi fallere, da iusto sanctoque uideri, noctem peccatis et fraudibus obice nubem.'
question: Quam deam fur tacite precatur ut fallere et iustus videri liceat, ut Horatius describit?
question_en: To which goddess does the thief pray under his breath, that he may deceive and yet seem just, as Horace describes?
derivation: Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves, with the whispered prayer that betrays the hypocrite. Anchored to the thief's prayer; one-name answer stated verbatim. Cult knowledge peculiar to Roman religion.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vir bonus et sapiens audebit dicere: 'Pentheu, rector Thebarum, quid me perferre patique indignum coges?'
question: Cuius urbis rex Pentheus fuit, quem Horatius loquentem inducit?
question_en: Of which city was Pentheus king, whom Horace brings on speaking?
derivation: Pentheus, king of Thebes and antagonist of Bacchus, in Horace's dramatic dialogue. Anchored by name; one-place answer stated verbatim. Shared myth of the tragic stage.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Opinor, hoc sentit: 'Moriar'. Mors ultima linea rerum est.
question: Quis poeta Romanus mortem ultimam rerum lineam esse dixit?
question_en: Which Roman poet said that death is the final line of all things?
derivation: Mors ultima linea rerum est, a much-quoted tag closing Epistulae 1.16; its checkable point is authorship. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Non cuiuis homini contingit adire Corinthum.
question: Ad quam urbem adire non cuivis homini contingere Horatius proverbio dicit?
question_en: To which city, in Horace's proverb, does it not fall to every man to go?
derivation: Horace's Latin rendering of the Greek proverb about Corinth's costly pleasures. Anchored to the proverb; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Nec semel inrisus triuiis attollere curat fracto crure planum, licet illi plurima manet lacrima, per sanctum iuratus dicat Osirim:
question: Per quem deum Aegyptium mendicus ille in triviis apud Horatium iurat?
question_en: By which Egyptian god does the beggar at the crossroads swear, in Horace?
derivation: The oath by Osiris in the mouth of a Roman street-beggar: the Egyptian cults in the city. Anchored to the crossroads beggar; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ambigitur quid enim? Castor sciat an Docilis plus, Brundisium Minuci melius uia ducat an Appi.
question: Quibus duabus viis Brundisium iri poterat, de quibus homines apud Horatium disputabant?
question_en: By which two roads could one travel to Brundisium, the point men disputed in Horace?
answer_en: By the Appian and the Minucian Way.
derivation: The two rival routes to Brundisium, a standard topic of Roman travellers' argument. Anchored to Brundisium; both road-names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Eutrapelus cuicumque nocere uolebat uestimenta dabat pretiosa; beatus enim iam cum pulchris tunicis sumet noua consilia et spes,
question: Quo dono Eutrapelus eos quibus nocere volebat corrumpebat?
question_en: By what gift did Eutrapelus ruin those he wished to harm?
derivation: The stratagem of Eutrapelus (P. Volumnius), a well-known Roman anecdote about the corrupting effect of finery. Anchored to the named man; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Zethi dissiluit, donec suspecta seuero conticuit lyra. Fraternis cessisse putatur moribus Amphion;
