question: Uter geminorum fratrum, Amphion an Zethus, lyram deposuit ut fratris moribus cederet?
question_en: Which of the twin brothers, Amphion or Zethus, laid down his lyre to yield to his brother's ways?
derivation: The Theban twins Amphion the lyre-player and Zethus the herdsman, the canonical pair of contrasting brothers. Anchored to both names; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sub duce qui templis Parthorum signa refigit nunc et, siquid abest, Italis adiudicat armis.
question: Quas res Romanas princeps ille, sub quo Lollius Cantabrica bella tulit, templis Parthorum refixit?
question_en: Which Roman things did the leader under whom Lollius served in the Cantabrian war take back from the temples of the Parthians?
derivation: The recovery of the standards lost at Carrhae, Augustus' celebrated Parthian settlement. Anchored to the Parthian temples + Lollius' commander; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: partitur lintres exercitus, Actia pugna te duce per pueros hostili more refertur; aduersarius est frater, lacus Hadria,
question: Cuius pugnae imaginem Lollius cum fratre per pueros in lacu paterno referebat?
question_en: Which battle did Lollius re-enact with his brother, using boys, on the lake of his father's estate?
derivation: The mock naval battle of Actium played on a country lake: Augustan spectacle turned into private game. Anchored to Lollius + his brother; the battle-name stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Consentire suis studiis qui crediderit te, fautor utroque tuum laudabit pollice ludum.
question: Quo gestu digitorum fautor apud Romanos ludum laudabat, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: By what gesture of the fingers did a Roman supporter show his approval of a display, as Horace says?
derivation: The thumb as the Roman sign of favour in the arena and at games (utroque pollice). Anchored to the fautor + the ludus; short answer stated verbatim. Spectacle custom, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Me quotiens reficit gelidus Digentia riuus, quem Mandela bibit, rugosus frigore pagus
question: Quo nomine appellatur rivus gelidus qui Horatium in Sabinis reficit, quem Mandela bibit?
question_en: What is the name of the cold stream that refreshes Horace in the Sabine country, from which Mandela drinks?
derivation: The Digentia and the village Mandela, the topography of Horace's Sabine farm. Anchored to Mandela + the Sabine estate; one name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Prisco si credis, Maecenas docte, Cratino, nulla placere diu nec uiuere carmina possunt quae scribuntur aquae potoribus;
question: Cuius poetae Graeci veteris auctoritate Horatius negat carmina ab aquae potoribus scripta diu placere posse?
question_en: On which old Greek poet's authority does Horace deny that poems written by water-drinkers can please for long?
derivation: Cratinus, the Old Comedy poet, cited by Horace for the dictum that water-drinkers write nothing lasting. Anchored to Horace + Maecenas + the dictum; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: laudibus arguitur uini uinosus Homerus;
question: Quem poetam Horatius ex vini laudibus vinosum fuisse arguit?
question_en: Which poet does Horace convict of being a wine-lover on the evidence of his praises of wine?
derivation: Horace's joke on Homer, standard ancient literary lore. Anchored to the praises of wine; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ennius ipse pater numquam nisi potus ad arma prosiluit dicenda.
question: Quem poetam Latinum Horatius 'patrem' appellat, qui numquam nisi potus ad arma dicenda prosiluit?
question_en: Which Latin poet does Horace call 'father', the one who never leapt to sing of arms unless he had been drinking?
derivation: Ennius pater, the honorific of the founder of Latin epic, with the anecdote of his drinking. Anchored to the epithet + the claim; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Parios ego primus iambos ostendi Latio, numeros animosque secutus Archilochi, non res et agentia uerba Lycamben;
question: Cuius poetae Parii numeros Horatius se primum Latio ostendisse gloriatur?
question_en: Whose Parian measures does Horace boast that he first showed to Latium?
derivation: Horace's claim to have naturalised Archilochean iambus at Rome (the Epodes). Anchored to Latium + the Parian iambi; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary history, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: numeros animosque secutus Archilochi, non res et agentia uerba Lycamben;
question: Quem virum Archilochi res et agentia verba egerunt, quas Horatius se non secutum esse profitetur?
question_en: Which man was hounded by Archilochus' matter and driving words, which Horace declares he did not follow?
derivation: Lycambes, whom Archilochus' iambics destroyed, the standing example of the poet's deadly invective. Anchored to Archilochus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: temperat Archilochi Musam pede mascula Sappho, temperat Alcaeus, sed rebus et ordine dispar,
question: Quos duos poetas Lesbios Horatius dicit Archilochi Musam eodem pede temperasse?
question_en: Which two poets of Lesbos does Horace say tempered Archilochus' Muse with the same foot?
derivation: The Lesbian pair, Sappho and Alcaeus, as heirs of Archilochus' metre: a fact about metrical descent that translates without residue. Anchored to Archilochus; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Hunc ego, non alio dictum prius ore, Latinus uolgaui fidicen;
question: Quo se nomine Horatius appellat, qui carmen Lesbium primus Latio vulgavit?
question_en: By what name does Horace call himself, as the first to publish Lesbian song for Latium?
derivation: Horace's celebrated self-designation as Latinus fidicen, claiming the Aeolic lyric (Alcaeus, named three lines above) for Rome. Anchored to Horace + Lesbian song; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vortumnum Ianumque, liber, spectare uideris, scilicet ut prostes Sosiorum pumice mundus.
question: Quorum librariorum tabernam Horatius nominat, ubi liber eius Romae venalis prostet?
question_en: Whose bookshop does Horace name as the place where his book will stand for sale at Rome?
derivation: The brothers Sosii, Horace's booksellers (cf. Ars Poetica 345, hic meret aera liber Sosiis). Anchored to Horace's book + the Roman book-trade; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: me primis urbis belli placuisse domique, corporis exigui, praecanum, solibus aptum, irasci celerem, tamen ut placabilis essem.
question: Qualem se corpore et capillo Horatius in fine libri primi Epistularum describit?
question_en: How does Horace describe his own body and hair at the end of the first book of the Epistles?
answer_en: Small of body and grey before his time.
derivation: Horace's famous self-portrait, the chief ancient evidence for his appearance. Anchored to Horace + the close of Epistles I; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Forte meum siquis te percontabitur aeuum, me quater undenos sciat impleuisse Decembris collegam Lepidum quo duxit Lollius anno.
question: Quot annos natus Horatius librum primum Epistularum absolvit, ut ipse in ultima epistula significat?
question_en: How old was Horace when he finished the first book of the Epistles, as he indicates in the last letter?
derivation: Horace dates his own age at the close of Epistles I: quater undenos Decembris, forty-four Decembers. Anchored to Horace + the book's close; a single number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: me quater undenos sciat impleuisse Decembris collegam Lepidum quo duxit Lollius anno.
question: Quibus consulibus Horatius se quater undenos Decembris implevisse scribit?
question_en: In whose consulship does Horace write that he completed forty-four Decembers?
answer_en: In the consulship of Lollius and Lepidus.
derivation: Roman dating by the consuls of the year (21 BC, when Lollius took Lepidus as colleague). Anchored to Horace's own dating; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Romulus et Liber pater et cum Castore Pollux, post ingentia facta deorum in templa recepti, dum terras hominumque colunt genus, aspera bella componunt, agros adsignant, oppida condunt,
question: Quos heroas Horatius nominat, qui post ingentia facta in deorum templa recepti sint?
question_en: Which heroes does Horace name as having been received into the temples of the gods after their mighty deeds?
answer_en: Romulus, Father Liber, Castor and Pollux.
derivation: The canonical list of mortals raised to divinity, cited by Horace to Augustus. Anchored to Horace's letter to Augustus; the four names stated verbatim. Religious-cultural knowledge, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Diram qui contudit hydram notaque fatali portenta labore subegit, comperit inuidiam supremo fine domari.
question: Quod monstrum Hercules apud Horatium contudit, cum fatali labore portenta subigeret?
question_en: Which monster did Hercules crush, in Horace, as he subdued the famous prodigies by his fated labour?
derivation: Hercules and the Hydra, one of the canonical labours. Anchored to Hercules + the labours; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Praesenti tibi maturos largimur honores iurandasque tuom per numen ponimus aras, nil oriturum alias, nil ortum tale fatentes.
question: Quid Romani principi adhuc vivo posuerunt, per cuius numen iurarent, ut Horatius ad Augustum scribit?
question_en: What did the Romans set up to their still-living emperor, to swear by his divine power, as Horace writes to Augustus?
derivation: The living emperor's altars and the oath by his numen: the institution of the imperial cult. Anchored to Augustus + the honours; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sic fautor ueterum ut tabulas peccare uetantis, quas bis quinque uiri sanxerunt, foedera regum uel Gabiis uel cum rigidis aequata Sabinis,
question: A quot viris tabulae legum Romanarum sanctae sunt, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: By how many men were the tablets of Roman law ratified, as Horace writes?
derivation: The Twelve Tables, drawn up by the decemviri: Horace's bis quinque uiri. Anchored to the tablets forbidding wrongdoing; a number answer stated verbatim. Foundational legal fact, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: foedera regum uel Gabiis uel cum rigidis aequata Sabinis, pontificum libros, annosa uolumina uatum
question: Quorum duorum populorum foedera cum regibus Romanis icta Horatius inter vetusta Romanorum monumenta numerat?
question_en: With which two peoples does Horace count the old treaties of the kings among Rome's ancient documents?
derivation: The treaty with Gabii and the treaty with the Sabines, the oldest documents of Roman public law. Anchored to the kings' treaties; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ennius, et sapiens et fortis et alter Homerus, ut critici dicunt, leuiter curare uidetur quo promissa cadant et somnia Pythagorea.
question: Quo cognomine critici Ennium ornabant, ut Horatius refert?
question_en: By what title did the critics honour Ennius, as Horace reports?
derivation: Ennius as alter Homerus, the standard verdict of the Roman critics (and an allusion to his Pythagorean dream). Anchored to Ennius + the critics; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Naeuius in manibus non est et mentibus haeret paene recens? Adeo sanctum est uetus omne poema.
question: Cuius veteris poetae carmina Horatius adhuc in manibus esse et paene recentia mentibus haerere dicit?
question_en: Which old poet's works does Horace say are still in men's hands and stick in their minds as if new?
derivation: Naevius still read at Rome in Horace's day: a fact of the Roman literary canon. Anchored to the old poets; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ambigitur quotiens uter utro sit prior, aufert Paccuuius docti famam senis, Accius alti,
question: Quam famam Pacuvius poeta apud Horatium aufert?
question_en: What reputation does the poet Pacuvius carry off, in Horace?
answer_en: That of the learned old man.
derivation: The canonical Roman verdicts on the early tragedians: Pacuvius the learned, Accius the lofty. Anchored to Pacuvius; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aufert Paccuuius docti famam senis, Accius alti,
question: Quo epitheto Accium tragicum Horatius ornat?
question_en: By what epithet does Horace honour the tragedian Accius?
derivation: Accius alti, the standing critical label for the greatest Roman tragedian. Anchored to Accius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: dicitur Afrani toga conuenisse Menandro, Plautus ad exemplar Siculi properare Epicharmi,
question: Cui comico Graeco Afranii togam convenisse dicebatur?
question_en: To which Greek comic poet was Afranius' toga said to be suited?
derivation: The Roman critical commonplace pairing Afranius (writer of togatae) with Menander. Anchored to Afranius; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Plautus ad exemplar Siculi properare Epicharmi, uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
question: Ad cuius Siculi poetae exemplar Plautum properare Horatius dicit?
question_en: On which Sicilian poet's model does Horace say Plautus hurries along?
derivation: Plautus measured against Epicharmus of Sicily, a fixed judgement of Roman criticism. Anchored to Plautus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
question: Qua virtute Caecilium comicum vincere Horatius dicit?
question_en: In what quality does Horace say the comic poet Caecilius wins?
derivation: The canonical verdict on Caecilius Statius. Anchored to Caecilius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
question: Qua virtute Terentium vincere Horatius dicit?
question_en: In what quality does Horace say Terence wins?
derivation: The canonical verdict on Terence, paired against Caecilius. Anchored to Terence; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: habet hos numeratque poetas ad nostrum tempus Liui scriptoris ab aeuo.
question: A cuius scriptoris aetate Roma poetas suos numerare Horatius dicit?
question_en: From which writer's age does Horace say Rome counts her poets?
derivation: Livius Andronicus as the starting-point of Latin literature. Anchored to Rome's roll of poets; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Non equidem insector delendaue carmina Liui esse reor, memini quae plagosum mihi paruo Orbilium dictare;
question: Quo magistro Horatius puer carmina Livi Andronici ediscebat?
question_en: Under which schoolmaster did the boy Horace learn the poems of Livius Andronicus?
derivation: Orbilius, Horace's schoolmaster, and the use of Livius Andronicus as a school text. Anchored to Horace's boyhood + Livius; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: memini quae plagosum mihi paruo Orbilium dictare;
question: Quo cognomine Horatius Orbilium magistrum suum notavit?
question_en: By what epithet did Horace brand his schoolmaster Orbilius?
derivation: Plagosus Orbilius, the proverbial flogging schoolmaster of Roman education. Anchored to Orbilius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Recte necne crocum floresque perambulet Attae fabula si dubitem, clament periisse pudorem cuncti paene patres,
question: Quibus rebus scaena Romana in ludis conspergebatur, per quas Attae fabula ambulabat?
question_en: With what was the Roman stage strewn at the games, through which Atta's play walked?
derivation: Saffron and flowers scattered on the Roman stage, a detail of theatrical luxury. Anchored to Atta's play + the stage; both items stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: cuncti paene patres, ea cum reprehendere coner quae grauis Aesopus, quae doctus Roscius egit,
question: Quos duos histriones nobilissimos Horatius nominat, quorum fabulas reprehendere paene nefas erat?
question_en: Which two most celebrated actors does Horace name, whose plays it was almost sacrilege to criticise?
derivation: Aesopus the tragic and Roscius the comic actor, the two great names of the Roman stage. Anchored to the Roman theatre; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Iam Saliare Numae carmen qui laudat, et illud quod mecum ignorat solus uolt scire uideri,
question: Cui regi carmen Saliare tribuebatur, quod Horatius laudari mirabatur?
question_en: To which king was the Salian hymn ascribed, which Horace marvels to hear praised?
derivation: The carmen Saliare, the archaic hymn of the Salian priests, ascribed to King Numa. Anchored to the hymn; one-name answer stated verbatim. Religious antiquity every Roman recognised.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Romae dulce diu fuit et sollemne reclusa mane domo uigilare, clienti promere iura, cautos nominibus rectis expendere nummos,
question: Quid Romae mane sollemne fuit erga clientem, cum domus reclusa esset?
question_en: What was the solemn morning practice at Rome toward a client, once the house was thrown open?
derivation: The morning salutatio: the patron opens his house at dawn and expounds the law to his clients. Anchored to Rome + the client; short answer stated verbatim. Central custom of Roman social life.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Mutauit mentem populus leuis et calet uno scribendi studio; pueri patresque seueri fronde comas uincti cenant et carmina dictant.
question: Qua re Romani inter cenam comas vinciebant, ut Horatius de scribendi studio queritur?
question_en: With what did Romans bind their hair at dinner, as Horace complains of the craze for writing?
derivation: Garlands of foliage worn by diners: the standing dress of the Roman dinner-party. Anchored to the cena; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: cum sociis operum pueris et coniuge fida Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
question: Qua hostia agricolae prisci Tellurem piabant, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: With what victim did the old farmers propitiate Earth (Tellus), as Horace writes?
derivation: The rustic harvest rite: the pig for Tellus. Anchored to the named deity + the old farmers; one-word answer stated verbatim. Sacrificial practice, the core of criterion 8.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
question: Qua re agricolae prisci Silvanum piabant, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: With what did the old farmers propitiate Silvanus, as Horace writes?
derivation: The milk offering to Silvanus, god of the woodland boundary. Anchored to the named deity; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
question: Quibus duabus rebus agricolae prisci Genium placabant, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: With which two things did the old farmers appease the Genius, as Horace writes?
derivation: The offering to the Genius at the harvest festival: flowers and wine, not blood. Anchored to the Genius; both items stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Fescennina per hunc inuenta licentia morem uersibus alternis opprobria rustica fudit,
question: Quo modo Fescennina licentia opprobria rustica inter agricolas fundebat?
question_en: In what form did Fescennine licence pour out its rustic abuse among the farmers?
derivation: The Fescennine verses, exchanged in alternate lines at country festivals: the origin Horace gives for Roman abusive verse. Anchored to the named licence; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: quin etiam lex poenaque lata, malo quae nollet carmine quemquam describi; uertere modum, formidine fustis ad bene dicendum delectandumque redacti.
question: Quid lex Romana de malo carmine sanxit, ut Horatius narrat?
question_en: What did the Roman law lay down about the malum carmen, as Horace tells it?
answer_en: That no one should be lampooned in an evil song.
derivation: The clause of the Twelve Tables penalising defamatory verse, which Horace makes the check on Fescennine abuse. Anchored to the law + the malum carmen; short answer stated verbatim. Legal fact, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Graecia capta ferum uictorem cepit et artes intulit agresti Latio;
question: Cuius poetae Romani est illud 'Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit', de artibus in Latium invectis?
question_en: Which Roman poet wrote 'captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive', of the arts brought into Latium?
derivation: The single most quoted line on Rome's conquest by Greek culture; its checkable point is authorship and subject (Horace, Epistulae 2.1, to Augustus). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sic horridus ille defluxit numerus Saturnius, et graue uirus munditiae pepulere;
question: Quo nomine appellatur ille horridus numerus, qui Graecis artibus in Latium invectis defluxit?
question_en: What was the name of the rough measure that ebbed away when Greek art came into Latium?
derivation: The Saturnian, the native Italian verse displaced by Greek metres: a fact about metre that names the metre and therefore translates without residue. Anchored to the arrival of Greek art; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Serus enim Graecis admouit acumina chartis et post Punica bella quietus quaerere coepit, quid Sophocles et Thespis et Aeschylos utile ferrent.
question: Post quae bella Romanus Graecis chartis acumina admovere coepit, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: After which wars did the Roman begin to apply his wits to Greek writings, as Horace writes?
derivation: Horace's dating of Rome's turn to Greek literature. Anchored to Rome + the Greek books; short answer stated verbatim. Literary-historical fact, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Aspice, Plautus quo pacto partis tutetur amantis ephebi, ut patris attenti, lenonis ut insidiosi,
question: Cuius poetae Romani personas — amantis ephebi, patris attenti, lenonis insidiosi — Horatius commemorat?
question_en: Which Roman poet's stock roles - the young lover, the tight-fisted father, the scheming pimp - does Horace recall?
derivation: The stock characters of Roman comedy as Horace lists them for Plautus. Anchored to the named roles; one-name answer stated verbatim. Theatrical convention, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: quantus sit Dossennus edacibus in parasitis, quam non adstricto percurrat pulpita socco;
question: Quo calceamento comoediae proprio Plautum pulpita percurrere Horatius dicit?
question_en: In what footwear proper to comedy does Horace say Plautus races over the boards?
derivation: The soccus, the low slipper of comedy as against the tragic cothurnus. Anchored to Plautus + the stage; one-word answer stated verbatim. Stage convention, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: indocti stolidique et depugnare parati si discordet eques, media inter carmina poscunt aut ursum aut pugiles; his nam plebecula gaudet.
question: Quid plebecula media inter carmina in theatro poscere solebat, ut Horatius ad Augustum queritur?
question_en: What did the crowd call for in the middle of a play, as Horace complains to Augustus?
derivation: The Roman audience interrupting a play to demand a bear-baiting or boxers. Anchored to the theatre crowd; short answer stated verbatim. Spectacle custom, the essence of criterion 8.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quattuor aut pluris aulaea premuntur in horas dum fugiunt equitum turmae peditumque cateruae;
question: Quot fere horas aulaea premuntur, dum equitum turmae peditumque catervae in scaena fugiunt?
question_en: For about how many hours is the curtain kept down while squadrons of horse and companies of foot flee across the stage?
derivation: The Roman stage-curtain (lowered, not raised) and the length of the spectacle-parades. Anchored to the theatre; a number answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Si foret in terris, rideret Democritus, seu diuersum confusa genus panthera camelo siue elephans albus uolgi conuerteret ora;
question: Quis philosophus, si in terris esset, spectacula Romana risurus erat, ut Horatius fingit?
question_en: Which philosopher, were he on earth, would laugh at the Roman shows, as Horace imagines?
derivation: Democritus the laughing philosopher, set by Horace in the Roman theatre. Anchored to the shows; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared cultural type.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: seu diuersum confusa genus panthera camelo siue elephans albus uolgi conuerteret ora;
question: Quae duo animalia peregrina Horatius nominat, quae vulgi ora in ludis converterent?
answer: Pantheram camelo confusam et elephantum album.
question_en: Which two foreign animals does Horace name as turning the crowd's faces at the games?
answer_en: A panther crossed with a camel (the giraffe) and a white elephant.
derivation: The exotic beasts displayed at Roman shows: the camelopard and the white elephant. Anchored to the games; both stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Dixit adhuc aliquid? Nil sane. Quid placet ergo? Lana Tarentino uiolas imitata ueneno.
question: Cuius urbis colore lana violas imitata tinguebatur, quae in scaena spectatoribus placebat?
question_en: With which city's dye was the wool coloured that imitated violets and delighted the audience on stage?
derivation: Tarentine purple, the famous dye of the Greek south of Italy, on stage costume. Anchored to the theatre + the wool; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Gratus Alexandro regi Magno fuit ille Choerilos, incultis qui uersibus et male natis rettulit acceptos, regale nomisma, Philippos.
question: Cui regi Choerilus poeta gratus fuit?
question_en: To which king was the poet Choerilus welcome?
derivation: Choerilus, Alexander's bad court poet, the standing example of a king's misplaced patronage. Anchored to Choerilus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: incultis qui uersibus et male natis rettulit acceptos, regale nomisma, Philippos.
question: Quo nomismate regio Choerilus poeta pro versibus suis donabatur?
question_en: In what royal coin was the poet Choerilus paid for his verses?
derivation: The Philippus, the gold coin of the Macedonian kings, named for Philip. Anchored to Choerilus + the royal coinage; one-word answer stated verbatim. Money knowledge, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: edicto uetuit nequis se praeter Apellen pingeret aut alius Lysippo duceret aera fortis Alexandri uoltum simulantia.
question: Quis pictor solus, Alexandri edicto, regem pingere permissus est?
question_en: Which painter alone was allowed by Alexander's edict to paint the king?
derivation: Alexander's edict reserving his portrait to Apelles: a famous fact of ancient art history. Anchored to Alexander's edict; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aut alius Lysippo duceret aera fortis Alexandri uoltum simulantia.
question: Cui soli artifici licuit Alexandri voltum ex aere ducere?
question_en: Which craftsman alone was permitted to cast Alexander's likeness in bronze?
derivation: Lysippus as Alexander's only authorised sculptor in bronze, the companion fact to Apelles. Anchored to Alexander's edict; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: At neque dedecorant tua de se iudicia atque munera, quae multa dantis cum laude tulerunt dilecti tibi Vergilius Variusque poetae,
question: Quos duos poetas Horatius Augusto dilectos nominat, qui munera eius cum laude acceperunt?
question_en: Which two poets does Horace name as dear to Augustus, who received his gifts to the giver's credit?
derivation: Virgil and Varius as the poets of Augustus' patronage. Anchored to Augustus + his gifts; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: claustraque custodem pacis cohibentia Ianum et formidatam Parthis te principe Romam,
question: Cuius dei claustra, pace parta, clausa cohibent, ut Horatius ad Augustum canit?
question_en: Which god do the bars shut in when peace has been won, as Horace sings to Augustus?
derivation: The closing of the gates of Janus in time of peace, one of the signal Augustan acts. Anchored to Augustus' peace; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: deferar in uicum uendentem tus et odores et piper et quicquid chartis amicitur ineptis.
question: Ad quas merces involvendas chartae ineptae adhibebantur, ut Horatius iocatur?
answer: Ad tus et odores et piper.
question_en: For wrapping what wares was useless writing-paper used, as Horace jokes?
derivation: The Roman joke that failed books end as wrapping in the spice-sellers' street. Anchored to the book trade; the three wares stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: 'Hic et candidus et talos a uertice pulcher ad imos fiet eritque tuus nummorum milibus octo,
question: Quanti pretii puer ille venalis in epistula Horati ad Florum offertur?
question_en: At what price is the slave boy offered for sale in Horace's letter to Florus?
derivation: The going price of a handsome, Greek-schooled slave boy: eight thousand sesterces. Anchored to Horace's letter + the sale; a single figure stated verbatim. Fact of the Roman slave market, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Luculli miles collecta uiatica multis aerumnis, lassus dum noctu stertit, ad assem perdiderat;
question: Cuius ducis miles, viatico noctu amisso, praesidium regale loco deiecit, ut Horatius narrat?
question_en: Whose soldier, after losing his savings in the night, dislodged a royal garrison, as Horace tells it?
derivation: The tale of Lucullus' soldier, the exemplum of poverty making men brave. Anchored to the named general; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Clarus ob id factum donis ornatur honestis, accipit et bis dena super sestertia nummum.
question: Quantam pecuniam miles ille Luculli pro forti facto accepit?
question_en: How much money did that soldier of Lucullus receive for his brave deed?
derivation: The soldier's reward, twice ten thousand sesterces over and above the decorations. Anchored to the soldier + Lucullus; a figure stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Post haec ille catus, quantumuis rusticus: 'Ibit, ibit eo, quo uis, qui zonam perdidit' inquit.
question: Quid miles ille praetori respondit, cum ad castellum expugnandum hortaretur?
answer: 'Ibit eo quo vis, qui zonam perdidit.'
question_en: What did the soldier answer the praetor who urged him to storm a fort?
answer_en: 'He will go where you like - the man who has lost his money-belt.'
derivation: The soldier's proverbial retort, the point of Horace's exemplum. Anchored to the soldier + the praetor; the saying quoted verbatim from the source.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Romae nutriri mihi contigit atque doceri iratus Grais quantum nocuisset Achilles. Adiecere bonae paulo plus artis Athenae,
question: In qua urbe Graeca Horatius studia sua auxit, Romae iam eruditus?
question_en: In which Greek city did Horace add to his studies, after his schooling at Rome?
derivation: Horace's education: Rome first, then Athens. Anchored to Horace + Rome; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Romae nutriri mihi contigit atque doceri iratus Grais quantum nocuisset Achilles.
question: Cuius herois ira Romae in ludo Horatio puero praelegebatur?
question_en: Which hero's wrath was read to the boy Horace in the schoolroom at Rome?
derivation: Homer's Iliad as the Roman schoolbook, described by its opening theme. Anchored to Roman schooling + Horace; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: scilicet ut uellem curuo dinoscere rectum atque inter siluas Academi quaerere uerum.
question: In quibus silvis Athenis Horatius verum quaerebat?
question_en: In which groves at Athens did Horace seek the truth?
derivation: The Academy, Plato's grove at Athens, where Horace studied. Anchored to Athens + Horace; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: ciuilisque rudem belli tulit aestus in arma Caesaris Augusti non responsura lacertis. Vnde simul primum me dimisere Philippi,
question: In quo proelio Horatius arma contra Caesarem Augustum tulisse et inde dimissus esse se fatetur?
question_en: In which battle does Horace admit he bore arms against Caesar Augustus and was thence discharged?
derivation: Horace's own testimony to his service on the losing side at Philippi. Anchored to Horace + Augustus; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: decisis humilem pinnis inopemque paterni et laris et fundi paupertas impulit audax ut uersus facerem;
question: Quae res Horatium, patrio lare et fundo amisso, ad versus faciendos impulit?
question_en: What drove Horace, stripped of his father's house and land, to make verses?
derivation: Horace's account of why he began to write: the confiscation after Philippi and consequent poverty. Anchored to Horace + the lost estate; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Frater erat Romae consulti rhetor, ut alter alterius sermone meros audiret honores, Gracchus ut hic illi, foret huic ut Mucius ille.
question: Quos duos viros Horatius exempla ponit, alterum eloquentiae, alterum iuris peritiae?
question_en: Which two men does Horace set up as models, one of eloquence, the other of legal learning?
derivation: Gracchus as the type of the orator, Mucius Scaevola as the type of the jurist: the Roman shorthand for the two professions. Anchored to the rhetor and the iuris consultus; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Caedimur et totidem plagis consumimus hostem, lento Samnites ad lumina prima duello.
question: Quod genus gladiatorum Horatius nominat, quorum lentum duellum ad lumina prima ducitur?
question_en: Which class of gladiators does Horace name, whose slow duel drags on till the lamps are lit?
derivation: The Samnis, one of the named gladiatorial types of the Roman arena. Anchored to the duel + the lamps; one-word answer stated verbatim. Spectacle knowledge, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Fuit haud ignobilis Argis, qui se credebat miros audire tragoedos in uacuo laetus sessor plausorque theatro,
question: Quid ille Argivus insanus in vacuo theatro sedens se audire credebat?
question_en: What did that madman of Argos, sitting in an empty theatre, believe he was hearing?
derivation: The famous Argive who applauded plays in an empty theatre, Horace's parable of happy delusion. Anchored to Argos + the empty theatre; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Hic ubi cognatorum opibus curisque refectus expulit elleboro morbum bilemque meraco et redit ad sese:
question: Quo medicamento ille Argivus insanus morbum bilemque expulit?
question_en: With what drug did that Argive madman drive out his disease and bile?
derivation: Hellebore as the ancient cure for madness (whence the proverbial Anticyra). Anchored to the Argive madman; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Si proprium est quod quis libra mercatus et aere est, quaedam, si credis consultis, mancipat usus,
question: Quibus duabus rebus adhibitis res apud Romanos mancipio emebatur, ut Horatius ad Florum scribit?
question_en: By the use of which two things was property bought by mancipation among the Romans, as Horace writes to Florus?
derivation: Mancipatio per aes et libram, the formal Roman conveyance. Anchored to Roman ownership + the jurists; both items stated verbatim. Legal institution, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: quaedam, si credis consultis, mancipat usus, qui te pascit ager, tuus est,
question: Quo modo, si iuris consultis credis, quaedam res sine mancipatione fiunt propriae, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: By what means, if you believe the jurists, do certain things become one's own without formal conveyance, as Horace says?
derivation: Usucapio, acquisition of ownership by long use, cited by Horace from the jurists. Anchored to the consulti; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sed uocat usque suum, qua populus adsita certis limitibus uicina refugit iurgia;
question: Quae arbor certis limitibus adserebatur, ut vicina iurgia refugerentur, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: Which tree was planted along fixed boundaries to keep off quarrels with the neighbours, as Horace writes?
derivation: Poplars planted as boundary markers on Italian farms. Anchored to the field boundaries; one-word answer stated verbatim. Agrarian custom, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: scit Genius, natale comes qui temperat astrum, naturae deus humanae, mortalis in unum quodque caput, uoltu mutabilis, albus et ater.
question: Qui deus, ut Horatius scribit, natale cuiusque astrum comes temperat?
question_en: Which god, as Horace writes, attends and governs each man's birth-star?
derivation: The Genius, the god born with each man and dying with him: the definition Horace gives. Anchored to the birth-star; one-word answer stated verbatim. Roman religion proper.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: ac potius, puer ut festis Quinquatribus olim, exiguo gratoque fruaris tempore raptim.
question: Quibus feriis pueri Romani a ludo litterario vacabant, quas Horatius exempli causa ponit?
question_en: At which festival did Roman schoolboys get their holiday, the one Horace cites as an example?
derivation: The Quinquatrus of March, Minerva's festival and the schoolboys' holiday. Anchored to Roman boys + the festival; one-word answer stated verbatim. Calendar knowledge.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Somnia, terrores magicos, miracula, sagas, nocturnos lemures portentaque Thessala rides?
question: Cuius regionis portenta Horatius inter magicos terrores numerat?
question_en: Which region's portents does Horace count among the terrors of magic?
derivation: Thessaly as the proverbial home of witchcraft in the Roman imagination. Anchored to the list of magical terrors; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Somnia, terrores magicos, miracula, sagas, nocturnos lemures portentaque Thessala rides?
question: Quo nomine Romani nocturnas umbras mortuorum appellabant, quas Horatius inter terrores numerat?
question_en: By what name did the Romans call the night-walking ghosts of the dead, which Horace lists among terrors?
derivation: The lemures, the Roman night-ghosts placated at the Lemuria. Anchored to the list of night terrors; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Lusisti satis, edisti satis atque bibisti; tempus abire tibi est,
question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit 'lusisti satis, edisti satis atque bibisti; tempus abire tibi est'?
question_en: Which Roman poet wrote 'you have played enough, eaten and drunk enough; it is time for you to go'?
derivation: The closing tag of the second book of Epistles, much quoted; its checkable point is authorship and place. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Humano capiti ceruicem pictor equinam iungere si uelit et uarias inducere plumas undique collatis membris, ut turpiter atrum desinat in piscem mulier formosa superne,
question: In quam bestiam mulier superne formosa desinit in illa pictura, qua Horatius Artem Poeticam incipit?
question_en: Into what creature does the woman, lovely above, end in the picture with which Horace opens the Ars Poetica?
derivation: The monstrous composite picture that opens the Ars Poetica, one of the best-known images in Latin criticism. Anchored to the opening of the work; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: "Pictoribus atque poetis quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas."
question: Quibus duobus artificibus par audendi potestas semper fuisse dicitur, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
question_en: Which two kinds of craftsman have always had, as the Ars Poetica quotes it, an equal licence to dare anything?
derivation: The famous claim quoted (and qualified) by Horace, endlessly cited in later criticism. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; both named verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Inceptis grauibus plerumque et magna professis purpureus, late qui splendeat, unus et alter adsuitur pannus,
question: Quo colore est pannus ille, qui gravibus inceptis adsui solet, ut Horatius in Arte Poetica dicit?
question_en: What colour is the patch that is commonly sewn onto grave beginnings, as Horace says in the Ars Poetica?
derivation: The purpureus pannus, origin of the phrase 'purple patch'. Anchored to Horace's criticism of irrelevant ornament; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Amphora coepit institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?
question: Quid ex rota currente exit, cum amphora institui coepta sit, ut Horatius quaerit?
question_en: What comes off the spinning wheel, when a wine-jar was begun, as Horace asks?
derivation: The potter's image for a work that changes shape in the making, a proverbial line. Anchored to the amphora + the wheel; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Aemilium circa ludum faber imus et unguis exprimet et mollis imitabitur aere capillos,
question: Quem ludum gladiatorium Romae Horatius nominat, circa quem ille faber infimus opera fingebat?
question_en: Which gladiatorial school at Rome does Horace name, near which that lowest craftsman worked?
derivation: The ludus Aemilius, a landmark of Rome, with the bronze-workers' shops around it. Anchored to the named school; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ego cur, adquirere pauca si possum, inuideor, cum lingua Catonis et Enni sermonem patrium ditauerit et noua rerum nomina protulerit?
question: Quorum duorum virorum lingua sermonem patrium ditavisse et nova rerum nomina protulisse Horatius dicit?
question_en: By which two men's speech does Horace say the native tongue was enriched and new names for things brought forth?
derivation: Cato and Ennius as the enrichers of the Latin language, a standing claim of Roman literary history. Anchored to the two names; both stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Res gestae regumque ducumque et tristia bella quo scribi possent numero, monstrauit Homerus.
question: Quis poeta monstravit quo numero res gestae regum ducumque et tristia bella scribi possent?
question_en: Which poet showed in what measure the deeds of kings and captains and grim wars could be written?
derivation: Homer as the founder of the epic metre, in Horace's history of the genres. Anchored to the subject-matter of epic; one-name answer stated verbatim. Translatable fact about metre (the hexameter and its proper matter).

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Versibus impariter iunctis querimonia primum, post etiam inclusa est uoti sententia compos;
question: Quae materia primum versibus impariter iunctis, id est elegis, inclusa est, ut Horatius docet?
question_en: What matter was first enclosed in unequally paired verses, that is, in elegiacs, as Horace teaches?
derivation: The elegiac couplet's first use for lament and afterwards for the fulfilled vow. Anchored to the couplet; one-word answer stated verbatim. A fact about a metre's proper matter, and so translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: quis tamen exiguos elegos emiserit auctor, grammatici certant et adhuc sub iudice lis est.
question: De cuius generis carminis auctore grammatici certare et litem adhuc sub iudice esse Horatius dicit?
question_en: About the author of which kind of poem does Horace say the grammarians contend, the case still before the judge?
derivation: The disputed inventor of elegy, and the proverbial tag adhuc sub iudice lis est. Anchored to the grammarians' quarrel; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Archilochum proprio rabies armauit iambo;
question: Quo metro rabies Archilochum armavit, ut Horatius in Arte Poetica scribit?
question_en: With what metre did rage arm Archilochus, as Horace writes in the Ars Poetica?
derivation: Archilochus as inventor and master of the iambus. Anchored by name; one-word answer stated verbatim. A fact about metre that names the metre, hence translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: hunc socci cepere pedem grandesque coturni, alternis aptum sermonibus et popularis uincentem strepitus et natum rebus agendis.
question: Quem pedem tam socci quam grandes coturni ceperunt, sermonibus alternis aptum?
question_en: Which foot did both the comic slipper and the high tragic buskin take over, as suited to alternating dialogue?
derivation: The iambus as the metre of drama, comic and tragic alike. Anchored to soccus and cothurnus; one-word answer supported verbatim (hunc... pedem, the iambus of the line before). Translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Musa dedit fidibus diuos puerosque deorum et pugilem uictorem et equom certamine primum et iuuenum curas et libera uina referre.
question: Cui carminis generi Musa dedit divos, pugilem victorem, equum certamine primum, iuvenum curas vinaque referre?
question_en: To which kind of poetry did the Muse grant the telling of gods, victorious boxers, winning horses, young men's loves and wine?
derivation: The proper matter of lyric in Horace's division of the genres. Anchored to the listed subjects; short answer stated verbatim (fidibus).

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: indignatur item priuatis ac prope socco dignis carminibus narrari cena Thyestae.
question: Cuius viri cena exemplum rei tragicae apud Horatium est, quae humili sermone narrari non vult?
question_en: Whose dinner is Horace's example of tragic matter that refuses to be told in humble style?
derivation: The banquet of Thyestes, the standing type of tragic horror. Anchored to tragic decorum; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Interdum tamen et uocem comoedia tollit, iratusque Chremes tumido delitigat ore;
question: Quae persona comica apud Horatium irata tumido ore rixatur?
question_en: Which comic character, in Horace, rails in anger with swollen speech?
derivation: Chremes, the stock angry old man of Greek and Roman comedy. Anchored to comedy raising its voice; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: et tragicus plerumque dolet sermone pedestri Telephus et Peleus, cum pauper et exul uterque proicit ampullas et sesquipedalia uerba,
question: Quos duos heroas tragicos Horatius nominat, qui pauperes et exules ampullas proiciunt?
question_en: Which two tragic heroes does Horace name as poor exiles who throw away their bombast?
derivation: Telephus and Peleus, the canonical beggared heroes of the tragic stage. Anchored to tragic style; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Honoratum si forte reponis Achillem, impiger, iracundus, inexorabilis, acer iura neget sibi nata, nihil non arroget armis.
question: Qualem Achillem in scaenam reponi Horatius iubet?
question_en: What sort of Achilles does Horace require, if you bring him back on stage?
derivation: The canonical characterisation of Achilles, the model of consistent portrayal. Anchored to Achilles; the four epithets stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Sit Medea ferox inuictaque, flebilis Ino, perfidus Ixion, Io uaga, tristis Orestes.
question: Qualem Medeam in scaena esse Horatius iubet?
question_en: What sort of Medea does Horace require on stage?
derivation: Medea's canonical attributes in the list of stage characters. Anchored to Medea; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Sit Medea ferox inuictaque, flebilis Ino, perfidus Ixion, Io uaga, tristis Orestes.
question: Quo epitheto Ixiona Horatius in Arte Poetica notat?
question_en: By what epithet does Horace mark Ixion in the Ars Poetica?
derivation: Ixion the treacherous, whose betrayal of his father-in-law and of Jupiter is the canonical story. Anchored to the list of stage characters; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quid dignum tanto feret hic promissor hiatu? Parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus.
question: Quid nascetur, cum montes parturient, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
question_en: What will be born when the mountains go into labour, as the Ars Poetica has it?
derivation: One of the most quoted lines in Latin, Horace's mock of the grandiose opening. Anchored to the line's first half; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: "Dic mihi, Musa, uirum, captae post tempora Troiae qui mores hominum multorum uidit et urbes".
question: Cuius carminis Graeci principium Horatius Latine reddit verbis 'dic mihi, Musa, virum'?
question_en: Which Greek poem's opening does Horace render into Latin with the words 'tell me, Muse, of the man'?
derivation: Horace's Latin version of the first lines of the Odyssey, held up as the model of a modest beginning. Anchored to the quoted opening; one-name answer supported by the content of the quotation.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: semper ad euentum festinat et in medias res non secus ac notas auditorem rapit,
question: Quo modo Homerum auditorem rapere Horatius dicit, cum semper ad eventum festinet?
question_en: How does Horace say Homer sweeps his hearer along, always hastening to the outcome?
derivation: The phrase in medias res, coined here and used ever since of narrative technique. Anchored to Homer's practice; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: si plosoris eges aulaea manentis et usque sessuri donec cantor. "Vos plaudite" dicat.
question: Quibus verbis cantor in fine fabulae Romanae spectatores plaudere iubebat?
question_en: With what words did the cantor call for applause at the end of a Roman play?
derivation: The formula that closed Roman comedies (cf. the endings of Plautus and Terence). Anchored to the end of the play + the cantor; the formula quoted verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ne pueros coram populo Medea trucidet, aut humana palam coquat exta nefarius Atreus,
question: Quid Medeam coram populo in scaena facere Horatius vetat?
question_en: What does Horace forbid Medea to do on stage in front of the audience?
derivation: The rule that atrocities happen offstage, with Medea's child-murder as the example. Anchored to Medea + the stage; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic convention, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aut humana palam coquat exta nefarius Atreus, aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
question: Quis rex humana exta coquit, quod in scaena palam fieri Horatius vetat?
question_en: Which king cooks human flesh, a thing Horace forbids to be done openly on stage?
derivation: Atreus' cannibal banquet, the canonical horror of tragedy. Anchored to the stage prohibition; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
question: In quam bestiam Procne mutata est, ut Horatius commemorat?
question_en: Into what creature was Procne changed, as Horace recalls?
derivation: Procne's metamorphosis into a bird, canonical Greek myth. Anchored by name; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
question: In quam bestiam Cadmus mutatus est, ut Horatius commemorat?
question_en: Into what creature was Cadmus changed, as Horace recalls?
derivation: Cadmus turned into a serpent, the close of the Theban founder's story. Anchored by name; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Neue minor neu sit quinto productior actu fabula, quae posci uolt et spectanda reponi;
question: Quot actus fabulam habere oportere Horatius in Arte Poetica praecipit?
question_en: How many acts does Horace prescribe for a play in the Ars Poetica?
derivation: The five-act rule, the most influential single prescription of ancient dramatic theory. Anchored to the play that wants to be revived; a number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nec deus intersit, nisi dignus uindice nodus inciderit;
question: Quando deum in scaenam intervenire Horatius permittit?
question_en: When does Horace allow a god to intervene on stage?
answer_en: Only when a knot has arisen that deserves such a deliverer.
derivation: The rule of the deus ex machina. Anchored to the stage god; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic convention, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nec quarta loqui persona laboret.
question: Quot personae in scaena loqui debent, ut Horatius praecipit?
answer: Tres; quarta enim loqui non debet.
question_en: How many characters should speak on stage, by Horace's rule?
answer_en: Three; a fourth should not try to speak.
derivation: The three-actor rule of ancient drama, stated by Horace as the ban on a fourth speaking part. Anchored to the stage; short answer stated verbatim in substance (nec quarta loqui persona laboret).

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Actoris partis chorus officiumque uirile defendat, neu quid medios intercinat actus, quod non proposito conducat et haereat apte.
question: Quas partes chorum in fabula sustinere Horatius iubet?
question_en: What part does Horace require the chorus to sustain in a play?
answer_en: An actor's part and a man's duty.
derivation: The function of the dramatic chorus, and the ban on irrelevant interludes between acts. Anchored to the chorus; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Tibia non, ut nunc, orichalco uincta tubaeque aemula, sed tenuis simplexque foramine pauco adspirare et adesse choris erat utilis
question: Qualis olim tibia fuit, antequam orichalco vinciretur et tubae aemula fieret, ut Horatius describit?
question_en: What was the pipe like in the old days, before it was bound with brass and rivalled the trumpet, as Horace describes it?
answer_en: Thin and simple, with few holes.
derivation: The early Roman tibia, slender and few-holed, before theatrical music grew grand. Anchored to the old theatre; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Carmine qui tragico uilem certauit ob hircum, mox etiam agrestis Satyros nudauit et asper incolumi grauitate iocum temptauit
question: Quod vile praemium olim in tragici carminis certamine petebatur, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: What cheap prize was once competed for in the contest of tragic song, as Horace writes?
derivation: The goat-prize of the tragic contest, the standard ancient explanation of the name 'tragedy'. Anchored to the contest; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: inlecebris erat et grata nouitate morandus spectator functusque sacris et potus et exlex.
question: Quales spectatores novitate Satyrorum morandi erant, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: What sort of spectators had to be held by the novelty of the satyr-play, as Horace says?
answer_en: Those who had finished the rites, drunk and lawless.
derivation: The satyr play placed after the tragedies to hold an audience fresh from the sacrifices and the wine. Anchored to the satyr play; short answer stated verbatim. Festival-theatre custom.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: ut nihil intersit Dauusne loquatur et audax Pythias, emuncto lucrata Simone talentum, an custos famulusque dei Silenus alumni.
question: Quis in fabulis Satyricis custos et famulus dei alumni inducitur?
question_en: Who is brought on in satyr plays as guardian and servant of the god he nursed?
derivation: Silenus, tutor of the young Bacchus and standing character of the satyr play. Anchored to the satyr drama; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nec sic enitar tragico diferre colori ut nihil intersit Dauusne loquatur et audax Pythias, emuncto lucrata Simone talentum,
question: Quo nomine servus comicus apud Horatium exempli causa appellatur?
question_en: By what name is the comic slave called in Horace's example?
derivation: Davus, the canonical name of the slave in Roman comedy (as in Terence). Anchored to comic characters; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: offenduntur enim quibus est equos et pater et res, nec, siquid fricti ciceris probat et nucis emptor, aequis accipiunt animis donantue corona.
question: Quas res humiliores spectatores in ludis emere solebant, ut Horatius indicat?
question_en: What did the humbler spectators buy at the shows, as Horace indicates?
derivation: The cheap snacks of the Roman theatre crowd, set against the knights with horse, father and property. Anchored to the audience; both items stated verbatim. Food-and-spectacle culture.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Syllaba longa breui subiecta uocatur iambus, pes citus; unde etiam trimetris adcrescere iussit nomen iambeis, cum senos redderet ictus,
question: Quot ictus versus iambicus trimeter reddit, ut Horatius docet?
question_en: How many beats does the iambic trimeter render, as Horace teaches?
derivation: The iambic trimeter is so called though it yields six beats (three double feet). A fact about metre statable in any language, hence on the translatable track. Anchored to the named verse; a number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vos exemplaria Graeca nocturna uersate manu, uersate diurna.
question: Quae exemplaria Horatius Pisones nocturna diurnaque manu versare iubet?
question_en: Which models does Horace tell the Pisos to thumb by night and by day?
derivation: The programmatic command of the Ars Poetica, endlessly quoted. Anchored to Horace + the Pisos; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: At uestri proaui Plautinos et numeros et laudauere sales, nimium patienter utrumque, ne dicam stulte, mirati,
question: Cuius poetae numeros et sales proavi Pisonum nimium patienter laudaverunt, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: Whose measures and whose jests did the Pisos' forefathers praise far too tolerantly, as Horace says?
derivation: Horace's verdict on Plautus and on the old Romans' taste. Anchored to the ancestors' praise; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary history, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ignotum tragicae genus inuenisse Camenae dicitur et plaustris uexisse poemata Thespis
question: Quis tragoediae genus ignotum invenisse et plaustris poemata vexisse dicitur?
question_en: Who is said to have invented the unknown kind of tragic song and carried his poems about on wagons?
derivation: Thespis, inventor of tragedy and the wagon-stage, in the standard ancient account. Anchored to the invention of tragedy; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: dicitur et plaustris uexisse poemata Thespis quae canerent agerentque peruncti faecibus ora.
question: Qua re histriones apud Thespin ora perunguebant, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: With what did Thespis' performers smear their faces, as Horace writes?
derivation: The lees-smeared faces of the earliest tragic performers, before the mask. Anchored to Thespis; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Post hunc personae pallaeque repertor honestae Aeschylus et modicis instrauit pulpita tignis
question: Quis personae pallaeque honestae repertor fuisse dicitur, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: Who is said to have been the inventor of the mask and the noble robe, as Horace writes?
derivation: Aeschylus credited with the tragic mask, the stately costume and the raised stage. Anchored to the invention; one-name answer stated verbatim. Theatre history, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Aeschylus et modicis instrauit pulpita tignis et docuit magnumque loqui nitique coturno.
question: Quo calceamento niti histriones Aeschylus docuit?
question_en: In what footwear did Aeschylus teach actors to stride?
derivation: The cothurnus as the mark of tragedy, taught by Aeschylus (against the comic soccus). Anchored to Aeschylus; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Successit uetus his comoedia, non sine multa laude; sed in uitium libertas excidit et uim dignam lege regi; lex est accepta chorusque turpiter obticuit sublato iure nocendi.
question: Quid Veteri Comoediae accidit, lege accepta, ut Horatius narrat?
question_en: What happened to Old Comedy when the law was passed, as Horace tells it?
derivation: The silencing of the Old Comic chorus once a law curbed its licence to injure. Anchored to Old Comedy + the law; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic history, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nec minimum meruere decus uestigia Graeca ausi deserere et celebrare domestica facta, uel qui praetextas uel qui docuere togatas.
question: Quibus duobus fabularum generibus poetae Romani domestica facta celebraverunt, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: By which two kinds of play did Roman poets celebrate home-grown deeds, as Horace says?
derivation: The two native Roman dramatic genres: the praetexta (historical) and the togata (Roman-dress comedy). Anchored to the Roman poets; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vos, o Pompilius sanguis, carmen reprehendite quod non multa dies et multa litura coercuit atque praesectum deciens non castigauit ad unguem.
question: Quotiens ad unguem castigatum esse carmen Horatius postulat?
question_en: How many times over does Horace require a poem to have been trimmed to the fingernail?
derivation: The demand for repeated correction, source of the phrase ad unguem. Anchored to the Pisos + the poem; a number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ingenium misera quia fortunatius arte credit et excludit sanos Helicone poetas Democritus, bona pars non unguis ponere curat, non barbam, secreta petit loca, balnea uitat;
question: Quis philosophus sanos poetas Helicone excludere creditur, ingenium arti praeferens?
question_en: Which philosopher is believed to shut sane poets out of Helicon, preferring genius to art?
derivation: Democritus' doctrine of poetic madness, the source of the unkempt poet's pose. Anchored to Helicon + the doctrine; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: nanciscetur enim pretium nomenque poetae, si tribus Anticyris caput insanabile nunquam tonsori Licino commiserit.
question: Quot Anticyrae caput poetae furentis sanare non possint, ut Horatius iocatur?
question_en: How many Anticyras, in Horace's joke, could not cure the mad poet's head?
derivation: Anticyra, the town of hellebore, is the proverbial cure for madness; three of them would not serve. Anchored to the mad poet; a number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Scribendi recte sapere est et principium et fons.
question: Quam rem Horatius scribendi recte et principium et fontem esse dicit?
question_en: What does Horace call both the beginning and the fountainhead of writing well?
derivation: A much-quoted Horatian tag; its checkable point is what stands in the predicate. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Romani pueri longis rationibus assem discunt in partis centum diducere.
question: In quot partes Romani pueri assem diducere discebant, ut Horatius scribit?
question_en: Into how many parts did Roman boys learn to divide the as, as Horace writes?
derivation: The Roman schoolroom's arithmetic of fractions of the as. Anchored to Roman boys + the as; a number stated verbatim. Education and money, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: filius Albini: si de quincunce remota est uncia, quid superat?. . . Poteras dixisse. — Triens. — Eu!
question: Quid superat, si de quincunce uncia remota est, ut in ludo Romano discebatur?
question_en: What is left if an ounce is taken from a quincunx, as was learned in the Roman schoolroom?
derivation: The fractions of the as: quincunx (5/12) less uncia (1/12) leaves triens (4/12). Anchored to the school exercise; the answer stated verbatim. Money-reckoning every Roman carried.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Rem poteris seruare tuam. Redit uncia, quid fit? "Semis".
question: Quid fit, si ad quincuncem uncia redit, ut in ludo Romano respondebatur?
question_en: What do you get if the ounce is added back to the quincunx, as the Roman schoolroom answered?
derivation: The second half of the schoolroom sum: quincunx (5/12) plus uncia (1/12) makes semis (6/12). Anchored to the same exercise; the answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Aut prodesse uolunt aut delectare poetae aut simul et iucunda et idonea dicere uitae.
question: Quid poetas velle Horatius in Arte Poetica dicit?
question_en: What does Horace say poets want to do, in the Ars Poetica?
answer_en: Either to profit or to please.
derivation: The formula that governed later criticism (prodesse et delectare). Anchored to the poets; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ficta uoluptatis causa sint proxima ueris, ne quodcumque uolet poscat sibi fabula credi, neu pransae Lamiae uiuum puerum extrahat aluo.
question: Cuius monstri alvo puer vivus extrahi non debet, ut Horatius vetat?
question_en: From what monster's belly must a living boy not be dragged, in Horace's prohibition?
derivation: Lamia, the child-devouring bogey of ancient nursery tale. Anchored to the stage prohibition; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Centuriae seniorum agitant expertia frugis, celsi praetereunt austera poemata Ramnes.
question: Quo nomine Horatius iuvenes equites appellat, qui austera poemata praetereunt?
question_en: By what name does Horace call the young knights who pass over austere poems?
derivation: Ramnes, one of the three original centuries of Roman knights, used for the young nobility of the theatre audience. Anchored to the audience; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci, lectorem delectando pariterque monendo;
question: Quis omne punctum tulit, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
question_en: Who has won every vote, as the Ars Poetica has it?
answer_en: He who has mixed the useful with the sweet.
derivation: One of the most quoted lines of the Ars Poetica; the image is of the ballot-marks (puncta). Anchored to the line's opening; short answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: et idem indignor quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus; uerum operi longo fas est obrepere somnum.
question: Quem poetam Horatius interdum dormitare dicit, cum de operis longi maculis loquitur?
question_en: Which poet does Horace say sometimes nods, when he speaks of the blemishes of a long work?
derivation: Quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus, proverbial ever since. Anchored to the quoted line; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vt pictura poesis; erit quae, si propius stes, te capiat magis, et quaedam, si longius abstes;
question: Cui arti Horatius poesin in Arte Poetica comparat?
question_en: To which art does Horace compare poetry in the Ars Poetica?
derivation: Ut pictura poesis, the tag that founded a whole tradition of criticism. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: sed tamen in pretio est; mediocribus esse poetis non homines, non di, non concessere columnae.
question: Qui tres poetis mediocribus esse non concesserunt, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: Which three have refused poets leave to be middling, as Horace says?
answer_en: Men, gods and the booksellers' pillars.
derivation: The famous denial of middling poetry, with the columnae (the pillars where books were advertised) as the third judge. Anchored to poets; the three stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vt gratas inter mensas symphonia discors et crassum unguentum et Sardo cum melle papauer offendunt,
question: Cuius insulae mel amarum inter cenae offensiones Horatius numerat?
question_en: Which island's bitter honey does Horace count among the offences of a dinner?
derivation: Sardinian honey, proverbially bitter, served with poppy-seed. Anchored to the dinner table; the item stated verbatim. Food knowledge, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Ludere qui nescit, campestribus abstinet armis, indoctusque pilae disciue trochiue quiescit, ne spissae risum tollant impune coronae;
question: Quibus tribus ludis Romani in Campo exercebantur, quos Horatius nominat?
question_en: In which three games did Romans exercise on the Campus, as Horace names them?
derivation: The standard exercises of the Campus Martius. Anchored to the Campus; the three stated verbatim. Leisure custom, translatable.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Tu nihil inuita dices faciesue Minerua; id tibi iudicium est, ea mens.
question: Qua dea invita nihil dicendum aut faciendum esse Horatius monet?
question_en: Against which goddess's will does Horace warn one to say or do nothing?
derivation: The proverb invita Minerva, of working against one's natural gift. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Siquid tamen olim scripseris, in Maeci descendat iudicis auris et patris et nostras, nonumque prematur in annum membranis intus positis;
question: In quotum annum carmen premi Horatius iubet antequam edatur?
question_en: Until which year does Horace order a poem to be kept back before publication?
derivation: Nonum prematur in annum, the most quoted counsel of literary patience. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; a number stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: delere licebit quod non edideris; nescit uox missa reuerti.
question: Quid, semel emissum, reverti nescire Horatius dicit?
question_en: What, once let go, does Horace say cannot come back?
derivation: Nescit uox missa reuerti, a proverbial line on the irrevocability of publication. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Siluestris homines sacer interpresque deorum caedibus et uictu foedo deterruit Orpheus, dictus ob hoc lenire tigris rabidosque leones;
question: Quis vates tigris rabidosque leones lenisse dicitur, qui homines silvestris a caedibus deterruit?
question_en: Which bard is said to have soothed tigers and raging lions, having turned wild men from slaughter?
derivation: Orpheus as civiliser and tamer of beasts, canonical myth. Anchored by the deeds; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: dictus et Amphion, Thebanae conditor urbis, saxa mouere sono testudinis et prece blanda ducere quo uellet.
question: Quis Thebanae urbis conditor saxa sono testudinis movisse dicitur?
question_en: Which founder of the city of Thebes is said to have moved stones by the sound of his lyre?
derivation: Amphion building Thebes with his lyre, canonical myth. Anchored to Thebes; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Post hos insignis Homerus Tyrtaeusque mares animos in Martia bella uersibus exacuit,
question: Quos duos poetas Horatius dicit versibus mares animos in Martia bella exacuisse?
question_en: Which two poets does Horace say sharpened manly spirits for the wars of Mars with their verses?
derivation: Homer and Tyrtaeus as the martial poets in Horace's account of poetry's civic uses. Anchored to the deed; both names stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: abstinuit uenere et uino; qui Pythia cantat tibicen, didicit prius extimuitque magistrum.
question: In quibus certaminibus Graecis canit ille tibicen, quem Horatius exemplum laboris ponit?
question_en: At which Greek games does the piper play whom Horace holds up as an example of training?
derivation: The Pythian games at Delphi, where the pipers competed. Anchored to the piper; the games named verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vt qui conducti plorant in funere dicunt et faciunt prope plura dolentibus ex animo, sic derisor uero plus laudatore mouetur.
question: Qui homines in funere Romano plura quam ex animo dolentes faciunt, ut Horatius dicit?
question_en: Who, at a Roman funeral, weep and do almost more than those who truly grieve, as Horace says?
derivation: The hired mourners of the Roman funeral, whose grief outdoes the family's. Anchored to the funeral; one-word answer stated verbatim. Funerary custom.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Quintilio siquid recitares: "Corrige, sodes, hoc" aiebat "et hoc"; melius te posse negares, bis terque expertum frustra; delere iubebat
question: Quis criticus, cum quid ei recitaretur, 'corrige, sodes, hoc et hoc' dicere solebat, ut Horatius narrat?
question_en: Which critic used to say 'correct this, please, and this' when something was recited to him, as Horace tells it?
derivation: Quintilius Varus, the honest critic of the Augustan circle (mourned in Odes 1.24). Anchored to the recitation; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: arguet ambigue dictum, mutanda notabit, fiet Aristarchus, nec dicet: "Cur ego amicum offendam in nugis?"
question: Cuius grammatici Graeci nomen Horatius pro severo carminum iudice ponit?
question_en: Which Greek scholar's name does Horace use for the severe judge of poems?
derivation: Aristarchus of Samothrace, the Homeric critic, as the byword for rigorous textual judgement. Anchored to the honest critic; one-name answer stated verbatim.

author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica
source_text: Vt mala quem scabies aut morbus regius urget aut fanaticus error et iracunda Diana, uesanum tetigisse timent fugiuntque poetam,
question: Cuius deae ira apud Horatium inter mentis morbos numeratur?
question_en: Which goddess's anger does Horace count among the diseases of the mind?
