derivation: The famous dictum reported by his nephew. Anchored to the elder Pliny; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: 'nullus est liber tam malus...' is a standing Latin proverb.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: In itinere quasi solutus ceteris curis, huic uni vacabat: ad latus notarius cum libro et pugillaribus, cuius manus hieme manicis muniebantur, ut ne caeli quidem asperitas ullum studii tempus eriperet; qua ex causa Romae quoque sella vehebatur.
question: Quibus manus notarii Plini maioris hieme muniebantur, ne studendi tempus periret?
question_en: With what were the hands of the elder Pliny's shorthand-writer protected in winter, so that no study-time should be lost?
derivation: The secretary taking dictation on the road, his hands sleeved against the cold. Anchored to the elder Pliny + his notarius; stated verbatim. Closed-book: dictation to a notarius is the standard Roman mode of composition, and this is its most famous illustration.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: ut ne caeli quidem asperitas ullum studii tempus eriperet; qua ex causa Romae quoque sella vehebatur.
question: Quo vehiculo Plinius maior Romae vehebatur, ne studiis tempus deesset?
question_en: In what conveyance did the elder Pliny travel about Rome so as not to lose time for study?
derivation: The sella (litter-chair) used so that reading could continue in the streets. Anchored to the elder Pliny; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the sella and lectica are the standard means of getting about Rome for a man of rank.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Hac intentione tot ista volumina peregit electorumque commentarios centum sexaginta mihi reliquit, opisthographos quidem et minutissimis scriptos; qua ratione multiplicatur hic numerus.
question: Quot commentarios electorum Plinius maior nepoti suo reliquit?
question_en: How many notebooks of excerpts did the elder Pliny leave to his nephew?
derivation: The 160 notebooks of excerpts, written on both sides in minute hand. Anchored to the elder Pliny + his nephew; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the excerpt-notebooks are the emblem of ancient scholarly method.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Referebat ipse potuisse se, cum procuraret in Hispania, vendere hos commentarios Larcio Licino quadringentis milibus nummum; et tunc aliquanto pauciores erant.
question: Quanti Larcius Licinus commentarios Plini maioris in Hispania emere voluit?
question_en: For how much did Larcius Licinus wish to buy the elder Pliny's notebooks in Spain?
derivation: The offer for the notebooks while the elder Pliny was procurator in Spain. Anchored to the two named men; the sum is stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is the best-known price ever quoted for a set of ancient scholarly papers, equal to the equestrian census.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Emi autem non ut haberem domi, neque enim ullum adhuc Corinthium domi habeo, verum ut in patria nostra celebri loco ponerem, ac potissimum in Iovis templo; videtur enim dignum templo dignum deo donum.
question: In cuius dei templo Plinius signum Corinthium in patria sua ponere statuit?
question_en: In which god's temple did Pliny decide to place the Corinthian bronze in his home town?
derivation: Pliny's dedication of a purchased Corinthian bronze in the temple of Jupiter at Comum. Anchored to Pliny + his patria; stated verbatim. Closed-book: dedicating art in a temple as a civic gift is the standard Roman form of benefaction.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Est enim nudum, nec aut vitia si qua sunt celat, aut laudes parum ostentat. Effingit senem stantem; ossa musculi nervi, venae rugae etiam ut spirantis apparent.
question: Quam figuram signum Corinthium a Plinio emptum effingebat?
question_en: What figure did the Corinthian bronze bought by Pliny represent?
derivation: The realistic bronze of a standing old man. Anchored to Pliny's purchase; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the description is the best-known Latin account of an individual bronze statue and of Roman connoisseurship of Corinthium aes.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Modo nuntiatus est Silius Italicus in Neapolitano suo inedia finisse vitam. Causa mortis valetudo. Erat illi natus insanabilis clavus, cuius taedio ad mortem irrevocabili constantia decucurrit.
question: Quo genere mortis Silius Italicus poeta vitam finivit?
question_en: By what kind of death did the poet Silius Italicus end his life?
derivation: Silius' voluntary death by abstinence in his Neapolitan villa. Anchored to the named poet; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the death of the author of the Punica is a standard biographical fact.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Multum ubique librorum, multum statuarum, multum imaginum, quas non habebat modo, verum etiam venerabatur, Vergili ante omnes, cuius natalem religiosius quam suum celebrabat.
question: Cuius poetae natalem Silius Italicus religiosius quam suum celebrabat?
question_en: Whose birthday did Silius Italicus celebrate more devoutly than his own?
derivation: Silius' cult of Virgil, keeping the poet's birthday as a holy day. Anchored to the two named poets; stated verbatim. Closed-book: birthday observance (dies natalis) is a Roman religious practice, and Silius' Virgil-worship is his best-known trait.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Vergili ante omnes, cuius natalem religiosius quam suum celebrabat, Neapoli maxime, ubi monimentum eius adire ut templum solebat.
question: In qua urbe Silius Italicus monimentum Vergili ut templum adire solebat?
question_en: In which city did Silius Italicus visit Virgil's tomb as though it were a temple?
derivation: Virgil's tomb at Naples treated as a shrine. Anchored to Silius + Virgil + the city; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Virgil's Neapolitan tomb is one of the celebrated literary monuments of Italy.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Laeserat famam suam sub Nerone, credebatur sponte accusasse, sed in Vitelli amicitia sapienter se et comiter gesserat, ex proconsulatu Asiae gloriam reportaverat.
question: Cuius provinciae proconsulatu Silius Italicus gloriam reportavit?
question_en: From the proconsulship of which province did Silius Italicus win glory?
derivation: Silius' governorship of Asia, the most prestigious senatorial province. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the proconsulate of Asia is the summit of a senatorial career and a well-known point of Silius' biography.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: utque novissimus a Nerone factus est consul, ita postremus ex omnibus, quos Nero consules fecerat, decessit. Illud etiam notabile: ultimus ex Neronianis consularibus obiit, quo consule Nero periit.
question: Quo insigni anno Silius Italicus consulatum gessit?
question_en: In what notable year did Silius Italicus hold the consulship?
answer_en: The year in which Nero perished.
derivation: Silius consul in 68, the year of Nero's death, and the last of Nero's consuls to die. Anchored to Silius + Nero; stated verbatim. Closed-book: dating by consulships and the fall of Nero are shared Roman historical furniture.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: In hac tranquillitate annum quintum et septuagensimum excessit, delicato magis corpore quam infirmo.
question: Quem annum aetatis Silius Italicus excessit?
question_en: What year of his life had Silius Italicus passed?
derivation: Silius' age at death. Anchored to the named poet; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact about a canonical Latin epic poet.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: nam ferunt Xersen, cum immensum exercitum oculis obisset, illacrimasse, quod tot milibus tam brevis immineret occasus.
question: Quis rex, ut Plinius refert, immensum exercitum suum contemplatus illacrimasse fertur?
question_en: Which king, as Pliny relates, is said to have wept as he looked over his vast army?
derivation: The famous tears of Xerxes reviewing his host (Herodotus 7.45-46). Anchored to the named king; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is one of the best-known anecdotes of ancient history, cited as a commonplace on mortality.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nuper L. Piso, pater Pisonis illius, qui Valerio Festo per summum facinus in Africa occisus est, dicere solebat neminem se videre in senatu, quem consul ipse sententiam rogavisset.
question: A quo Piso ille in Africa per summum facinus occisus est?
question_en: By whom was that Piso murdered in Africa by an outrageous crime?
derivation: The killing of the proconsul Piso in Africa by Valerius Festus in 70. Anchored to the two named men + the province; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the episode belongs to the well-known aftermath of the civil wars of 69.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Facis pro cetera reverentia quam mihi praestas, quod tam sollicite petis ut tribunatum, quem a Neratio Marcello clarissimo viro impetravi tibi, in Caesennium Silvanum propinquum tuum transferam.
question: A quo Plinius Suetonio Tranquillo tribunatum militum impetravit?
question_en: From whom did Pliny obtain a military tribunate for Suetonius Tranquillus?
derivation: The commission got for Suetonius from the consular Neratius Marcellus. Anchored to the named parties; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the equestrian military tribunate as a patronage gift is standard Roman career practice, and Suetonius' is a famous instance.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Facis pro cetera reverentia quam mihi praestas, quod tam sollicite petis ut tribunatum, quem a Neratio Marcello clarissimo viro impetravi tibi, in Caesennium Silvanum propinquum tuum transferam.
question: In quem propinquum suum Suetonius Tranquillus tribunatum a Plinio impetratum transtulit?
question_en: To which of his relatives did Suetonius Tranquillus transfer the tribunate Pliny had obtained for him?
derivation: The transfer of the commission before the name was entered on the rolls (in numeros relatum). Anchored to Suetonius + the named kinsman; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it illustrates the real workings of military appointment, and the biographer Suetonius is a culturally salient figure.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Caecilius Classicus, homo foedus et aperte malus, proconsulatum in ea non minus violenter quam sordide gesserat, eodem anno quo in Africa Marius Priscus. Erat autem Priscus ex Baetica, ex Africa Classicus.
question: Cuius provinciae proconsulatum Caecilius Classicus violenter et sordide gessit?
question_en: The proconsulship of which province did Caecilius Classicus administer with violence and greed?
derivation: The second great repetundae case of Pliny's career, that of Classicus in Baetica. Anchored to the named governor; the province is stated verbatim. Closed-book: Baetica, Spain's senatorial province, and its prosecutions of governors are standard imperial history.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Erat autem Priscus ex Baetica, ex Africa Classicus. Inde dictum Baeticorum, ut plerumque dolor etiam venustos facit, non illepidum ferebatur: 'Dedi malum et accepi.'
question: Quod dictum Baeticorum de Mario Prisco et Caecilio Classico ferebatur?
question_en: What saying of the Baeticans was current about Marius Priscus and Caecilius Classicus?
answer_en: 'I gave a bad man and got one back.'
derivation: The Baeticans' quip: their own countryman Priscus ruined Africa, while the African Classicus ruined Baetica. Anchored to the two named governors and their provinces; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: the exchange-of-scoundrels joke is the memorable tag of the two trials.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Sua manu reliquerat scriptum, quid ex quaque re, quid ex quaque causa accepisset; miserat etiam epistulas Romam ad amiculam quandam, iactantes et gloriosas, his quidem verbis: 'Io io, liber ad te venio; iam sestertium quadragiens redegi parte vendita Baeticorum.'
question: Quantam pecuniam Caecilius Classicus se parte Baeticorum vendita redegisse gloriabatur?
question_en: How much money did Caecilius Classicus boast he had made by selling off part of the Baeticans?
derivation: The governor's boasting letter to his mistress, produced in evidence. Anchored to the named man + province; the sum is quoted verbatim. Closed-book: the scale of provincial extortion is a defining fact of Roman governance.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Erat in consilio Sertorianum illud exemplum, qui robustissimum et infirmissimum militem iussit caudam equi, reliqua nosti. Nam nos quoque tam numerosum agmen reorum ita demum videbamus posse superari, si per singulos carperetur.
question: Cuius ducis exemplum Plinius affert, qui milites caudam equi vellere iussit?
question_en: Which general's example does Pliny cite, who ordered soldiers to pull off a horse's tail?
derivation: Sertorius' demonstration that what cannot be torn off at once yields hair by hair. Anchored to the named general; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the horse-tail exemplum is one of the standard didactic anecdotes of Roman history.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Consilii nostri exitus fuit: bona Classici, quae habuisset ante provinciam, placuit senatui a reliquis separari, illa filiae haec spoliatis relinqui. Additum est, ut pecuniae quas creditoribus solverat revocarentur.
question: Quae bona Caecilii Classici senatus filiae eius relinqui iussit?
question_en: Which of Caecilius Classicus' goods did the senate order to be left to his daughter?
answer_en: Those he had held before his province.
derivation: The senate separating pre-provincial property from the proceeds of extortion, the latter going to the plundered. Anchored to the named man + the senate's decree; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the principle of restitution under the repetundae law is a real and salient legal rule.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Hispanus et Probus in quinquennium relegati; adeo grave visum est, quod initio dubitabatur an omnino crimen esset. Post paucos dies Claudium Fuscum, Classici generum, et Stilonium Priscum, qui tribunus cohortis sub Classico fuerat, accusavimus dispari eventu: Prisco in biennium Italia interdictum, absolutus est Fuscus.
question: In quot annos Baebius Probus et Fabius Hispanus, socii Classici, relegati sunt?
question_en: For how many years were Baebius Probus and Fabius Hispanus, the accomplices of Classicus, relegated?
derivation: The five-year relegation of the governor's agents. Anchored to the named men; stated verbatim. Closed-book: relegation for a fixed term is a standard penalty of Roman senatorial justice.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Norbanum Licinianum, legatum et inquisitorem, reum postulavit, tamquam in causa Castae, uxor haec Classici, praevaricaretur. Est lege cautum ut reus ante peragatur, tunc de praevaricatore quaeratur, videlicet quia optime ex accusatione ipsa accusatoris fides aestimatur.
question: Quo ordine lex de praevaricatore quaeri iubebat?
question_en: In what order did the law require an inquiry into a collusive prosecutor?
answer_en: After the defendant's case had been completed.
derivation: The rule of procedure on praevaricatio (collusive prosecution). Anchored to the Classicus trial and the named legate; stated verbatim. Closed-book: praevaricatio is a named offence of Roman criminal procedure.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Damnatus et in insulam relegatus est. Itaque cum Castam accusarem nihil magis pressi, quam quod accusator eius praevaricationis crimine corruisset; pressi tamen frustra; accidit enim res contraria et nova, ut accusatore praevaricationis damnato rea absolveretur.
question: Quo eventu novo causa Castae, uxoris Classici, terminata est?
answer: Accusatore praevaricationis damnato, rea absoluta est.
question_en: With what unprecedented outcome did the case of Casta, wife of Classicus, end?
answer_en: The prosecutor was condemned for collusion, yet the defendant was acquitted.
derivation: The paradoxical verdict Pliny singles out as new. Anchored to the named woman + her prosecutor Norbanus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is the memorable legal curiosity of the Baetican trials.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Equidem, cum essent philosophi ab urbe summoti, fui apud illum in suburbano, et quo notabilius, hoc est, periculosius, esset fui praetor.
question: Quo magistratu fungens Plinius Artemidorum philosophum adiit, cum philosophi ab urbe summoti essent?
question_en: While holding which magistracy did Pliny visit the philosopher Artemidorus at the time when philosophers had been expelled from the city?
derivation: The expulsion of the philosophers from Rome under Domitian, and Pliny's visit to one of them while praetor. Anchored to Pliny + Artemidorus; both facts stated verbatim. Closed-book: the banishment of philosophers is a famous recurring act of imperial policy.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Atque haec feci, cum septem amicis meis aut occisis aut relegatis, occisis Senecione Rustico Helvidio, relegatis Maurico Gratilla Arria Fannia, tot circa me iactis fulminibus quasi ambustus mihi quoque impendere idem exitium certis quibusdam notis augurarer.
question: Quot amici Plinii illo Domitiani tempore aut occisi aut relegati sunt?
question_en: How many of Pliny's friends were either killed or relegated in that period of Domitian's reign?
derivation: The seven friends struck down in Domitian's last terror. Anchored to Pliny and the named victims; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the persecution of the 'Stoic opposition' in 93 is standard imperial history.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: cum septem amicis meis aut occisis aut relegatis, occisis Senecione Rustico Helvidio, relegatis Maurico Gratilla Arria Fannia.
question: Qui tres ex amicis Plinii sub Domitiano occisi sunt?
question_en: Which three of Pliny's friends were put to death under Domitian?
derivation: Herennius Senecio, Arulenus Rusticus and Helvidius Priscus, executed in 93. Anchored to Pliny's list; all three named verbatim. Closed-book: they are the canonical martyrs of the senatorial opposition, also central to Tacitus' Agricola.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: cum septem amicis meis aut occisis aut relegatis, occisis Senecione Rustico Helvidio, relegatis Maurico Gratilla Arria Fannia.
question: Qui quattuor ex amicis Plinii sub Domitiano relegati sunt?
question_en: Which four of Pliny's friends were relegated under Domitian?
derivation: The four exiles, including the women of the Thrasea-Helvidius family. Anchored to Pliny's list; all four named verbatim. Closed-book: the exile of Fannia and Arria is a well-known episode of the reign.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nam et C. Musonium socerum eius, quantum licitum est per aetatem, cum admiratione dilexi et Artemidorum ipsum iam tum, cum in Syria tribunus militarem, arta familiaritate complexus sum.
question: Cuius philosophi gener fuit Artemidorus?
question_en: Whose son-in-law was the philosopher Artemidorus?
derivation: Artemidorus chosen as son-in-law by Musonius Rufus out of all his followers. Anchored to the two named philosophers; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Musonius Rufus is the best-known Roman Stoic teacher of the age.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Erunt officia antelucana, in quae incidere impune ne Catoni quidem licuit, quem tamen C. Caesar ita reprehendit ut laudet. Describit enim eos, quibus obvius fuerit, cum caput ebrii retexissent, erubuisse; deinde adicit: 'Putares non ab illis Catonem, sed illos a Catone deprehensos.'
question: Quis de Catone scripsit 'putares non ab illis Catonem, sed illos a Catone deprehensos'?
question_en: Who wrote of Cato, 'you would think it was not they who caught Cato, but Cato who caught them'?
derivation: Caesar's back-handed praise of Cato, from the Anticato. Anchored to Caesar + Cato; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: the Caesar-Cato antagonism and Caesar's pamphlet against him are shared republican history.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Rem atrocem nec tantum epistula dignam Larcius Macedo vir praetorius a servis suis passus est, superbus alioqui dominus et saevus, et qui servisse patrem suum parum, immo nimium meminisset. Lavabatur in villa Formiana. Repente eum servi circumsistunt.
question: Quo loco Larcius Macedo, vir praetorius, a servis suis oppressus est?
question_en: In what place was Larcius Macedo, a man of praetorian rank, set upon by his own slaves?
answer_en: In the bath of his villa at Formiae.
derivation: The murderous assault on Larcius Macedo by his household slaves while bathing. Anchored to the named man + his Formian villa; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the fear of one's own slaves is a standing Roman social anxiety, and this letter is its classic document.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Rem atrocem nec tantum epistula dignam Larcius Macedo vir praetorius a servis suis passus est, superbus alioqui dominus et saevus, et qui servisse patrem suum parum, immo nimium meminisset.
question: Quid de patre Larci Macedonis Plinius memorat?
question_en: What does Pliny record about the father of Larcius Macedo?
answer_en: That he had been a slave.
derivation: Macedo, a praetorian senator whose father had been a slave. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book and salient: the rise of the sons of freedmen into senatorial rank is a real and much-noticed feature of imperial society.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cum in publico Romae lavaretur, notabilis atque etiam, ut exitus docuit, ominosa res accidit. Eques Romanus a servo eius, ut transitum daret, manu leviter admonitus convertit se nec servum, a quo erat tactus, sed ipsum Macedonem tam graviter palma percussit ut paene concideret.
question: Quo loco eques Romanus Larcium Macedonem palma percussit?
question_en: Where did a Roman knight strike Larcius Macedo with the flat of his hand?
answer_en: In a public bath at Rome.
derivation: The earlier insult in the public baths, which Pliny reads as an omen of Macedo's death in his private bath. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the crowded public bath, where rank was jostled, is a central institution of Roman daily life.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Confirmata est opinio mea hesterno Fanniae sermone. Neptis haec Arriae illius, quae marito et solacium mortis et exemplum fuit.
question: Quo gradu Fannia ab Arria illa, Caecinae Paeti uxore, orta erat?
question_en: In what degree of descent did Fannia stand to the famous Arria, wife of Caecina Paetus?
derivation: The line Arria - Arria the younger - Fannia, the women of the Thrasea-Helvidius house. Anchored to both named women; stated verbatim. Closed-book: this family is the most famous dynasty of the senatorial opposition.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Aegrotabat Caecina Paetus maritus eius, aegrotabat et filius, uterque mortifere, ut videbatur. Filius decessit eximia pulchritudine pari verecundia, et parentibus non minus ob alia carus quam quod filius erat. Huic illa ita funus paravit, ita duxit exsequias, ut ignoraret maritus; quin immo quotiens cubiculum eius intraret, vivere filium atque etiam commodiorem esse simulabat.
question: Quam rem Arria a marito Caecina Paeto aegrotante celavit?
question_en: What did Arria conceal from her sick husband Caecina Paetus?
derivation: Arria arranging her son's funeral in secret so that her sick husband should not learn of it. Anchored to Arria + Paetus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is the story Pliny presents as greater than the famous dagger, and both belong to the shared repertory of Roman exempla.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Praeclarum quidem illud eiusdem, ferrum stringere, perfodere pectus, extrahere pugionem, porrigere marito, addere vocem immortalem ac paene divinam: 'Paete, non dolet.'
question: Quibus verbis Arria pugionem e pectore suo extractum marito porrexit?
question_en: With what words did Arria hand her husband the dagger drawn from her own breast?
derivation: The most famous words spoken by a Roman woman. Anchored to Arria + Paetus; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: 'Paete, non dolet' is a proverbial saying of Roman fortitude (also in Martial 1.13).

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Scribonianus arma in Illyrico contra Claudium moverat; fuerat Paetus in partibus, et occiso Scriboniano Romam trahebatur.
question: In qua provincia Scribonianus arma contra Claudium movit?
question_en: In which province did Scribonianus take up arms against Claudius?
derivation: The revolt of Camillus Scribonianus in Dalmatia/Illyricum in AD 42. Anchored to the named rebel + emperor; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the rising is a well-known episode of Claudius' reign and the frame of the Arria story.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Non impetravit: conduxit piscatoriam nauculam, ingensque navigium minimo secuta est.
question: Quo navigio Arria maritum captum Romam navi tractum secuta est?
question_en: In what vessel did Arria follow her captive husband as he was carried to Rome by ship?
derivation: Arria hiring a fisherman's skiff to follow her husband's warship. Anchored to Arria + Paetus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is one of the celebrated details of the Arria legend.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Quin etiam, cum Thrasea gener eius deprecaretur, ne mori pergeret, interque alia dixisset: 'Vis ergo filiam tuam, si mihi pereundum fuerit, mori mecum?', respondit: 'Si tam diu tantaque concordia vixerit tecum quam ego cum Paeto, volo.'
question: Quis fuit Arriae gener?
question_en: Who was Arria's son-in-law?
derivation: Thrasea Paetus married to Arria's daughter. Anchored to both named persons; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Thrasea Paetus, the Stoic senator forced to die under Nero, is one of the best-known figures of the period.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Dum haec dicit, exsiluit cathedra adversoque parieti caput ingenti impetu impegit et corruit. Focilata 'Dixeram' inquit 'vobis inventuram me quamlibet duram ad mortem viam, si vos facilem negassetis.'
question: Quo modo Arria mortem sibi consciscere temptavit, cum attentius custodiretur?
question_en: How did Arria attempt to kill herself when she was being watched more closely?
answer_en: She dashed her head against the wall opposite.
derivation: Arria's demonstration that no guard could keep her from death. Anchored to the named woman; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the episode belongs to the standard telling of the Arria exemplum.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Officium consulatus iniunxit mihi, ut rei publicae nomine principi gratias agerem. Quod ego in senatu cum ad rationem et loci et temporis ex more fecissem, bono civi convenientissimum credidi eadem illa spatiosius et uberius volumine amplecti.
question: Quo munere fungens Plinius rei publicae nomine principi in senatu gratias egit?
question_en: In what office did Pliny render thanks to the emperor in the senate on behalf of the state?
derivation: The consular gratiarum actio, later expanded into the published Panegyricus. Anchored to Pliny + the emperor; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the consul's speech of thanks is a fixed institution, and Pliny's is the only one preserved.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: foedissimis insuper tempestatibus per biduum convenerunt, cumque modestia mea finem recitationi facere voluisset, ut adicerem tertium diem exegerunt.
question: Per quot dies Plinius librum gratiarum actionis amicis recitavit?
question_en: For how many days did Pliny recite his book of thanksgiving to his friends?
derivation: The three-day recitation of the expanded Panegyricus. Anchored to Pliny + the work; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the multi-day recitatio before invited friends is the standard mode of Roman publication.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Superest ut scias quanti videantur posse emi. Sestertio triciens, non quia non aliquando quinquagiens fuerint, verum et hac penuria colonorum et communi temporis iniquitate ut reditus agrorum sic etiam pretium retro abiit.
question: Quanti praedia agris Plinii vicina emi posse videbantur?
question_en: For how much did the estates neighbouring Pliny's land seem able to be bought?
derivation: The asking price of the neighbouring estates, down from five million. Anchored to Pliny's deliberation; the figure is stated verbatim. Closed-book: land prices and the shortage of tenant farmers are real, salient facts of the Italian economy.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Sunt ergo instruendi, eo pluris quod frugi, mancipiis; nam nec ipse usquam vinctos habeo nec ibi quisquam.
question: Quid Plinius de mancipiis vinctis in praediis suis affirmat?
question_en: What does Pliny assert about chained slaves on his estates?
answer_en: That he keeps none in chains.
derivation: Pliny's refusal to use chain-gang slave labour (servi vincti). Anchored to Pliny + his estates; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the chained agricultural slave and the ergastulum are a well-known institution of Roman farming, which Pliny pointedly avoids.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Meministine te saepe legisse, quantas contentiones excitarit lex tabellaria, quantumque ipsi latori vel gloriae vel reprehensionis attulerit? At nunc in senatu sine ulla dissensione hoc idem ut optimum placuit: omnes comitiorum die tabellas postulaverunt.
question: Quid senatores comitiorum die postulaverunt, ut suffragia tacita fierent?
question_en: What did the senators demand on election day, so that the voting should be silent?
derivation: The introduction of the secret ballot into senatorial elections, recalling the republican lex tabellaria. Anchored to the senate + election day; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the tabella and the ballot laws are famous institutions of Roman voting.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Supersunt senes ex quibus audire soleo hunc ordinem comitiorum: citato nomine candidati silentium summum; dicebat ipse pro se; explicabat vitam suam, testes et laudatores dabat vel eum sub quo militaverat, vel eum cui quaestor fuerat, vel utrumque si poterat.
question: Quos testes et laudatores candidatus antiquitus in senatu dare solebat?
answer: Eum sub quo militaverat vel eum cui quaestor fuerat.
question_en: Whom did a candidate of old bring forward in the senate as witnesses and commenders?
answer_en: The man under whom he had served, or the man whose quaestor he had been.
derivation: The old form of senatorial elections: the candidate speaking for himself and producing his commander or his consul as guarantors. Anchored to the senate's electoral custom; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the bond between a magistrate and his quaestor is a well-known feature of Roman public life.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Audio Valerium Martialem decessisse et moleste fero. Erat homo ingeniosus acutus acer, et qui plurimum in scribendo et salis haberet et fellis nec candoris minus.
question: Cuius poetae mortem Plinius Cornelio Prisco nuntiat?
question_en: Whose death as a poet does Pliny announce to Cornelius Priscus?
derivation: Pliny's obituary notice of the epigrammatist Martial. Anchored to the named poet; stated verbatim. Closed-book: this letter is the principal ancient evidence for Martial's death and for the friendship between the two writers.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Prosecutus eram viatico secedentem; dederam hoc amicitiae, dederam etiam versiculis, quos de me composuit.
question: Quid Plinius Martiali ab urbe secedenti dedit?
question_en: What did Pliny give Martial when he withdrew from the city?
derivation: Pliny paying Martial's fare home to Spain. Anchored to the two named men; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the viaticum given by a patron to a departing friend is a recognized Roman social courtesy.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Fuit moris antiqui eos, qui vel singulorum laudes vel urbium scripserant, aut honoribus aut pecunia honorare; nostris vero temporibus ut alia speciosa et egregia ita hoc in primis exolevit.
question: Quo more antiquo ii honorabantur, qui vel singulorum vel urbium laudes scripserant?
question_en: By what ancient custom were those honoured who had written the praises of individuals or of cities?
derivation: The old custom of rewarding panegyric poets with public honours or cash. Anchored to Pliny's report + the practice; stated verbatim. Closed-book: literary patronage and its rewards are central to Roman cultural life.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Alloquitur Musam, mandat, ut domum meam Esquiliis quaerat, adeat reverenter.
question: In quo Romae colle domum Plinii Martialis carmine suo Musam quaerere iubet?
question_en: On which hill of Rome does Martial in his poem bid his Muse seek Pliny's house?
derivation: Pliny's house on the Esquiline, as addressed in Martial 10.19. Anchored to Pliny + Martial; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the hills of Rome and their residents are shared topographical knowledge.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: totos dat tetricae dies Minervae, dum centum studet auribus virorum hoc, quod saecula posterique possint Arpinis quoque comparare chartis.
question: Cuius oratoris chartis Martialis Plinii scripta comparari posse dicit, cum eas Arpinas nominat?
question_en: To which orator's pages does Martial say Pliny's writings may be compared, when he calls them 'the pages of Arpinum'?
derivation: The periphrasis 'Arpinae chartae' for Cicero, born at Arpinum. Anchored to Martial's poem on Pliny; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Cicero's origin at Arpinum is standard shared knowledge, and the periphrasis presupposes it.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: totos dat tetricae dies Minervae, dum centum studet auribus virorum hoc, quod saecula posterique possint Arpinis quoque comparare chartis.
question: Cui deae Martialis Plinium totos dies dare dicit?
question_en: To which goddess does Martial say Pliny gives whole days?
derivation: Minerva as patroness of study and eloquence, contrasted in the same poem with Lyaeus of the evening. Anchored to Martial's verses on Pliny; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Minerva's patronage of learning is core Roman religious-cultural knowledge.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Seras tutior ibis ad lucernas; haec hora est tua, cum furit Lyaeus, cum regnat rosa, cum madent capilli. Tunc me vel rigidi legant Catones.
question: Quo cognomine Martialis in his versibus Bacchum appellat?
question_en: By what title does Martial call Bacchus in these verses?
derivation: Lyaeus ('the loosener'), a canonical cult-title of Bacchus, here standing for the wine of the evening hour. Anchored to Martial's poem; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the divine epithets of Bacchus are shared mythological knowledge, and the rose-garlands and scented hair of the drinking hour are the standard convivial scene.

author: Pliny the Elder
provenance: LacusCurtius (Mayhoff/Teubner edition) — NOT the Latin Library; this book is absent from the Latin Library corpus and was fetched separately, normalized to the corpus's plain-text style.
source_text: produntur Arimaspi, quos diximus, uno oculo in fronte media insignes. quibus adsidue bellum esse circa metalla cum grypis, ferarum volucri genere, quale vulgo traditur, eruente ex cuniculis aurum, mira cupiditate et feris custodientibus et Arimaspis rapientibus, multi, sed maxime inlustres Herodotus et Aristeas Proconnesius scribunt.
question: Quo corporis insigni Arimaspos notari Plinius tradit?
question_en: By what bodily peculiarity does Pliny say the Arimaspi are marked?
answer_en: By a single eye in the middle of the forehead.
derivation: The one-eyed Arimaspi of the far north, a fixture of ancient ethnography from Herodotus and Aristeas onward. Anchored to the named people; the answer is stated verbatim (uno oculo in fronte media insignes). Closed-book and part of the shared stock of ancient world-geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
provenance: LacusCurtius (Mayhoff/Teubner edition) — NOT the Latin Library; this book is absent from the Latin Library corpus and was fetched separately, normalized to the corpus's plain-text style.
source_text: quibus adsidue bellum esse circa metalla cum grypis, ferarum volucri genere, quale vulgo traditur, eruente ex cuniculis aurum, mira cupiditate et feris custodientibus et Arimaspis rapientibus, multi, sed maxime inlustres Herodotus et Aristeas Proconnesius scribunt.
question: Cum quo genere ferarum Arimaspos circa aurum adsidue bellare traditur?
question_en: With what kind of beasts are the Arimaspi said to wage continual war over gold?
derivation: The perpetual war of the Arimaspi with the gold-guarding griffins. Anchored to the named people; single answer (grypes) supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the best-known marvels of the ancient north, cited by Pliny from Herodotus and Aristeas.

author: Pliny the Elder
provenance: LacusCurtius (Mayhoff/Teubner edition) — NOT the Latin Library; this book is absent from the Latin Library corpus and was fetched separately, normalized to the corpus's plain-text style.
source_text: similis et in Africa Psyllorum gens fuit, ut Agatharchides scribit, a Psyllo rege dicta, cuius sepulcrum in parte Syrtium Maiorum est.
question: A quo rege gentem Psyllorum in Africa nomen accepisse Plinius tradit?
question_en: From which king does Pliny say the African people of the Psylli took their name?
derivation: The Psylli, the famous snake-charming people of the Syrtes, named from king Psyllus whose tomb lies by the Greater Syrtis. Anchored to the named people; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Psylli are a stock reference for snake-immunity in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder
provenance: LacusCurtius (Mayhoff/Teubner edition) — NOT the Latin Library; this book is absent from the Latin Library corpus and was fetched separately, normalized to the corpus's plain-text style.
source_text: horum corpori ingenitum fuit virus exitiale serpentibus et cuius odore sopirent eas; mos vero liberos genitos protinus obiciendi saevissimis earum eoque genere pudicitiam coniugum experiendi, non profugientibus adulterino sanguine natos serpentibus.
question: Quo more Psylli pudicitiam coniugum suarum experiri solebant?
question_en: By what custom did the Psylli test the chastity of their wives?
answer_en: By exposing their newborn children to snakes.
derivation: The Psyllan ordeal: infants were thrown to the fiercest snakes, which fled from children of adulterous blood. Anchored to the named people; the custom is stated verbatim (mos vero liberos genitos protinus obiciendi ... eoque genere pudicitiam coniugum experiendi).
